# Pryv compliance matrix

> Maps 15 regulations and standards (GDPR, HIPAA, Swiss nLPD, CCPA, PIPEDA, DiGA, MDR, HDS, ISO 27001, ISO 27701, ISO 13485, SOC 2 and more) requirement by requirement onto what Pryv, the platform built from open-pryv.io, implements, makes configurable, facilitates or documents, and what stays with the implementer. 439 requirements, each backed by evidence (tests, docs, configuration keys).

Use it to answer questions such as "does Pryv support GDPR Art. 17 erasure?" or "what is left for me to do for HIPAA 164.312(b)?". Start from the scope file, then follow its evidence links.

This matrix describes the software's contribution to compliance. It is not legal advice and not a certification: implementer organisations remain responsible for their own GDPR, HIPAA, ISO, MDR or HDS posture. Rows marked draft are authored but not yet reviewed.

## How to read a requirement

Coverage (what Pryv does for the implementer):
- `implemented`: Pryv ships the control out of the box; it works with no configuration.
- `configurable`: Pryv provides the control once the operator sets the configuration keys cited on the requirement.
- `facilitated`: Pryv reduces the work; the implementer still does part of it (see the facilitation mode).
- `documented`: Guidance only: the implementer does the work, following the cited documentation.
- `out-of-scope`: No software contribution from Pryv; the obligation, if any, stays with the implementer.

Effort saved (how much of the work Pryv carries):
- `high`: Pryv carries most of the engineering and operational work.
- `medium`: The work is roughly shared between Pryv and the implementer.
- `low`: Pryv contributes a small technical substrate; most of the work is the implementer's.

Facilitation mode (the kind of help, mostly on `facilitated` rows):
- `primitive`: Pryv's permissions, access versioning or system streams technically enforce the obligation; the implementer chooses the stream layout and permission scope.
- `evidence`: Pryv generates structured data (audit log, access version chain, event history) that the implementer uses as proof in an artefact they produce.
- `storage`: Pryv durably stores artefacts the implementer creates (notice text, consent records, policies) and makes them recoverable per subject and per time.
- `infrastructure`: Pryv runs the technical layer the obligation depends on (TLS, encryption at rest, high availability, data residency, backup and restore).
- `awareness`: Pryv has minimal direct contribution; the row reminds the implementer of the obligation.

Evidence: test codes resolve at https://pryv.github.io/tests/#<code>, functional specs at https://pryv.github.io/functional-specifications/ and docs paths at https://pryv.github.io/<path>/.


## California Consumer Privacy Act (as amended by CPRA) (CCPA / CPRA)

- Scope id: `ccpa` (regulation)
- Jurisdiction: US, California (extraterritorial via business-nexus thresholds)
- Version: Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1798.100 - 1798.199.100 (CPRA amendments operative) (2023-01-01)
- Official text: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?division=3.&part=4.&lawCode=CIV&title=1.81.5
- Requirements: 18 (3 implemented, 3 configurable, 9 facilitated, 3 out-of-scope)
- Browse: https://pryv.github.io/compliance-matrix/#/scope/ccpa

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.100: Right to know what personal information is collected

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Consumer has the right to request that a business that collects
personal information about the consumer disclose the categories,
sources, business / commercial purposes, and specific pieces
collected.

**What Pryv does for you**

Same Pryv mechanism as GDPR Art. 15: the consumer holding a
personal token reads events, streams, accesses, audit data via
the standard API. Categories + sources are encoded in the event
class/format (data-types) and event.clientData.source.
Business / commercial purpose is encoded in
`access.clientData.purpose` per access.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA01, EGSQ, UZEV
- specs: EVENT.BASE, STREAM.BASE
- derives from: gdpr.Art.15
- primitives: access, stream, event, audit, data-types

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.105: Right to delete personal information

Coverage: configurable · effort saved: medium · draft

Requirement: Consumer has the right to request deletion of personal information
collected from the consumer; with statutory exceptions (Section
1798.105(d)).

**What Pryv does for you**

Same primitive as GDPR Art. 17: `system.users.delete` is the
per-consumer erasure call. Backup-completeness of the deletion
depends on the chosen storage engine (SQLite per-user file vs
PG row deletion), same notes as gdpr.Art.17 apply. Since
open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.58 the deletion also releases the
consumer's external ids (links to third-party record ids) at
once, on the home core and in the platform index `[XIDD2]`. From
the release after open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.87 each deletion leaves a
durable record without the consumer's data (the erasure ledger,
see gdpr.Art.17), so you can confirm later that a consumer's
account was deleted, and when `[ERLG4]`, `[ERLA4]`. The
§1798.105(d) statutory exceptions (warranty, security, legal
compliance, etc.) are your programmatic determination; if an
exception applies you suppress the deletion and document why.

**Detail**

Account auto-deletion, since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.66
(`8521c8d5`, see gdpr.Art.17): the consumer can schedule the
deletion of their own account, at a date or after a period
without use, from the reference account app, where your
`user-account.delete` lets them delete it directly
(`[ACST10]`; arming needs the password, `[ACST3]`); reminders
precede it (`[ACRM1]`) and the deletion is the same as
`system.users.delete`, guards included (`[ADSW8]`). It has no
hook for a §1798.105(d) exception: if one applies to a consumer
whose deletion is scheduled, that is still your determination,
made before the deadline (for example by turning the feature off
on the core with `account.autoDeletion.enabled: false`, or by
your own process outside it).

**Evidence**

- tests: USAD, XIDD2, ACST3, ACST10, ADSW8, ACRM1, ERLG4, ERLA4
- docs: customer-resources/account-auto-deletion.md
- config keys: storages.userAccountStorage.engine, user-account.delete, account.autoDeletion.enabled
- derives from: gdpr.Art.17
- primitives: event, stream, backup-restore, external-id-index, account-auto-deletion

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.106: Right to correct inaccurate personal information

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Consumer has the right to request that a business correct
inaccurate personal information.

**What Pryv does for you**

`events.update` is the correction primitive, and the audit log
records who corrected which event and when. The prior
(inaccurate) value is kept for traceability only if your
deployment sets `versioning.forceKeepHistory: true` (off by
default; see `context/event-history.md`). The §1798.106 process
(consumer request → reasonable efforts → action) is yours to run;
the technical correction is shipped, and keeping the history is
your configuration choice.

**Evidence**

- tests: PTU1
- specs: EVENT.BASE
- derives from: gdpr.Art.16
- primitives: event
- context notes: event-history

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.110: Right to know, categories and specific pieces

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Consumer has the right to request specific categories of personal
information and the specific pieces of personal information the
business has collected about the consumer.

**What Pryv does for you**

Categories surface from the canonical event-type schemas
(`event.type` = `<class>/<format>`); specific pieces are the
events themselves. A consumer-portal app wrapping
`events.get`+`streams.get` delivers both in one response.

**Evidence**

- tests: EGSQ, UZEV
- specs: EVENT.BASE, STREAM.BASE
- derives from: gdpr.Art.15
- primitives: event, stream, data-types, account-backup-tool

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.115: Right to know about sale or sharing

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Consumer has the right to know whether personal information was
sold or shared, the categories sold or shared, and the categories
of third parties to whom it was sold or shared.

**What Pryv does for you**

Every "sale" or "sharing"
you do, in CCPA's broad sense, which includes cross-context
behavioural advertising, happens through a Pryv access granted
to the recipient. The access's `clientData` can carry the
§1798.115 classification (sale vs share, category of third
party); audit records anchor the transaction in time. What's
not the software's job: deciding when a use qualifies as "sale"
or "sharing" under the CCPA definition (Civ. Code §1798.140(ad)
+(ah)), that's a contractual / classification decision you
record on the access.

**Detail**

Pattern: when minting an access for a counterparty:
`access.clientData = {`
`  type: "share",          // or "sale", per §1798.140`
`  third_party_category: "ad_partner",`
`  contract_id: "..."`
`}`
The consumer-side §1798.115 response then queries
`accesses.get ?includeHistory=true` filtered on
`clientData.type ∈ {sale, share}` and surfaces the third-party
categories.

**Evidence**

- primitives: access, clientData, audit, CMC

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.120: Right to opt out of sale or sharing

Coverage: configurable · effort saved: medium · draft

Requirement: Consumer has the right, at any time, to direct a business that
sells or shares personal information about the consumer to third
parties not to do so.

**What Pryv does for you**

Opt-out is implemented by revoking or narrowing the access
powering the sale/share, `accesses.delete` for full opt-out,
`accesses.update` for narrowing, both versioned and audit-
anchored. A `consent/opt-out-sale-cmc` event (or custom
`optout/*` event) gives the consumer-side artefact alongside
the technical effect.

**Detail**

Honoring Global Privacy Control signals (which CPPA regulations
require treating as a §1798.120 opt-out request) is your
application-layer responsibility, detect the GPC header on the
consumer's browser session and trigger the access revoke flow
automatically. Pryv has no opinion on the signal source.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA02, ACCP
- config keys: access.permissions
- derives from: gdpr.Art.21
- primitives: access, permissions, clientData, audit

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.121: Right to limit use of sensitive personal information

Coverage: configurable · effort saved: medium · draft

Requirement: Consumer has the right to direct a business that collects
sensitive personal information to limit its use to what is
necessary to perform the services or provide the goods
reasonably expected (with statutory exceptions in CPPA
regulations).

**What Pryv does for you**

The limit-use directive is operationalized by narrowing the
relevant accesses' `permissions[]` to the minimum-necessary
streams. The "reasonably expected use" classification is your
programmatic decision; the technical control is the access
mutation. Sensitive personal information (per §1798.140(ae))
can be segregated onto designated streams up front so the
narrowing operation is a known-shape transformation.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA02, ACCP
- config keys: access.permissions
- derives from: gdpr.Art.18
- primitives: access, permissions, stream

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.125: Non-discrimination

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Business shall not discriminate against a consumer because the
consumer exercised any rights under CCPA.

**What Pryv does for you**

Non-discrimination is a business-policy commitment, pricing,
service levels, marketing eligibility, not a software control.
Pryv has no role in pricing or product gating; if your app
enforces tier-based feature access, the non-discrimination
analysis happens at your app's pricing-policy layer.

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.130: Notice and response procedures

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Business must provide notice of categories of PI collected,
purposes, sources; respond to verifiable consumer requests within
45 days (one extension permitted, 90 day total max).

**What Pryv does for you**

Notice text lives on
`access.clientData.privacy_notice` or on a dedicated
`consent/notice` event, preserved per consumer per time,
recoverable later. The 45-day response window is your
operational target. Pryv's read APIs respond in milliseconds,
so the rate-limit on the response is your fulfilment workflow,
not a software latency.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.12
- primitives: access, clientData, app-web-auth3, event

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.135: Methods for opt-out

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: awareness · draft

Requirement: Business must provide a clear "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal
Information" link / mechanism; CPRA additionally requires
honoring opt-out preference signals (Global Privacy Control).

**What Pryv does for you**

The opt-out UI surface is
your app, a CCPA-required link or an automated GPC-signal
handler. When the opt-out is exercised, the Pryv mechanism is
the access revoke / narrow flow from §1798.120. Implementer's
job: detect the opt-out, call the Pryv revoke flow, surface
confirmation.

**Evidence**

- primitives: access, clientData

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.140: Definitions

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: awareness · draft

Requirement: Defines key terms including "personal information", "sensitive
personal information", "sale", "sharing", "service provider",
"third party".

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv primitives map
cleanly to most CCPA-defined terms (event = personal-information
storage; access + permissions = the consent / authorization
layer; CMC = sharing across distinct operators). The
§1798.140(ae) sensitive-personal-information category drives
stream layout (segregate sensitive categories onto designated
subtrees for clean §1798.121 limit-use operation).

**Detail**

Service-provider vs third-party (§1798.140(ag) vs (ai))
classification is contractual, record it on the access's
`clientData.role` so the consumer-side §1798.115 response
surfaces the right category.

**Evidence**

- primitives: event, stream, access, clientData, CMC

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.150: Civil action for breach

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: Consumer whose nonencrypted and nonredacted personal information
is subject to an unauthorized access, exfiltration, theft, or
disclosure as a result of failure to maintain reasonable security
may bring a civil action for statutory damages ($100-$750 per
consumer per incident or actual damages).

**What Pryv does for you**

Two contributions:
(1) TLS-in-transit + operator-side at-rest encryption move ePHI
/ personal-information out of the "nonencrypted and nonredacted"
trigger zone for §1798.150; (2) audit + access-version data are
the technical evidence layer when defending a "reasonable
security" claim. The "reasonable security" determination remains
a fact-specific legal question; Pryv provides the substrate.

**Detail**

The §1798.150 trigger is narrow, encrypted-and-redacted PI
that leaks doesn't ground a statutory-damages claim. Pryv's
posture (TLS in the core or at your proxy, as you configure it
+ operator-side at-rest encryption + per-
access access-control + audit) substantially constrains the
surface where §1798.150 can attach. Encryption-at-rest is
operator-side (LUKS, PG TDE, etc.) for event content today;
Pryv-managed at-rest encryption covers platform secrets.

**Evidence**

- primitives: letsEncrypt-integration, encryption-at-rest-secrets, audit, access

**Planned changes**

- feature: End-to-end encryption narrows the §1798.150 nonencrypted-PI trigger zone further

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.81.5: Reasonable security procedures (Cal. Civ. Code §1798.81.5)

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: high · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: Business that owns, licenses, or maintains personal information
about a California resident shall implement and maintain
reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the
nature of the information, to protect the information from
unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or
disclosure.

**What Pryv does for you**

Statute predates CCPA
but provides the "reasonable security" basis the §1798.150 civil
action attaches to. Pryv's multi-aspect technical baseline (TLS,
mTLS, at-rest secrets, audit, MFA, backup-restore, permissions)
constitutes the software-layer "reasonable security" inventory.
The organizational-side reasonable-security programme is the
operator's.

**Evidence**

- derives from: ccpa.1798.150, gdpr.Art.32
- primitives: access, permissions, audit, letsEncrypt-integration, encryption-at-rest-secrets, MFA, backup-restore

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.130(a)(5): Notice, content elements

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Privacy-policy notice must include categories of PI collected,
categories of sources, business / commercial purposes, categories
of third parties with whom PI is shared, sale / sharing
practices, and consumer rights.

**What Pryv does for you**

Notice content is editorial.
Pryv preserves the notice text per individual consumer (on
`account.clientData.privacy_notice` or a dedicated event), so
the precise wording shown at the moment a particular consumer
first interacted is recoverable later. Drafting the wording
remains the implementer's editorial work.

**Evidence**

- derives from: ccpa.1798.130
- primitives: access, clientData

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.135(a): Methods for opt-out, Do Not Sell / Share + Limit Use links

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Business that sells or shares PI shall provide a clear and
conspicuous link titled "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal
Information" on its homepage. Business that uses sensitive PI for
purposes beyond those listed in §1798.121(a) shall provide an
additional link titled "Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal
Information".

**What Pryv does for you**

The UI link is part of the implementer's homepage; Pryv is the
backend the link's handler talks to (revoke / narrow the
relevant access). Surface itself is app-layer.

**Evidence**

- derives from: ccpa.1798.135, ccpa.1798.120

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.140(ad): Definition, "Sale"

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: "Sale" / "Sell" includes selling, renting, releasing, disclosing,
disseminating, making available, transferring, or otherwise
communicating orally, in writing, or by electronic / other
means, a consumer's personal information by the business to
another business or a third party for monetary or other valuable
consideration.

**What Pryv does for you**

Whether a given access
constitutes a "sale" under §1798.140(ad) is a classification the
implementer applies + records on the access's
`clientData.type = "sale"`. The consideration test (monetary or
valuable) is fact-specific and editorial; Pryv preserves
whatever classification you record.

**Evidence**

- derives from: ccpa.1798.140
- primitives: access, clientData

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.140(ae): Definition, "Sensitive personal information"

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: primitive · draft

Requirement: Enumerated categories: SSN, drivers license, account log-in
with password, precise geolocation, racial / ethnic origin,
religious / philosophical beliefs, union membership, contents
of mail / email / text messages not directed at the business,
genetic data, biometric identifier, health, sex life or
sexual orientation.

**What Pryv does for you**

Sensitive-PI enumeration
drives stream-layout design, dedicate subtrees per sensitive
category (`sensitive/health/`, `sensitive/precise-location/`,
etc.) for clean §1798.121 limit-use enforcement. The
classification of whether a specific event qualifies as
sensitive PI is editorial. An alias-only deployment pattern is now
available: issue accesses with `randomAlias:true` so counterparties
hold a routable `r-XXXXXXXX` alias instead of a linkable username,
keeping linkable identifiers off the sensitive-PI access path.
Since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.69 the token is accepted under its
alias only, so a counterparty that suspects the username cannot
confirm it with the token; earlier releases accepted the token
under every name of the account.

**Evidence**

- derives from: ccpa.1798.121, gdpr.Art.9
- primitives: stream, system-streams, event, randomAlias

### CCPA / CPRA 1798.155: Enforcement

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA) + California Attorney
General may bring civil actions for CCPA violations; statutory
penalties up to $2,500 per violation ($7,500 for intentional
violations + violations involving minors).

**What Pryv does for you**

Enforcement is regulator-side. No software role; Pryv's audit
log + access-version chain are the evidence pack the implementer
surfaces in response to inquiries.


## Data Governance (DAMA-DMBOK knowledge areas) (Data Governance)

- Scope id: `data-governance` (discipline)
- Jurisdiction: International (framework)
- Version: DAMA-DMBOK 2 (framing) + ISO/IEC 38505-1 (2017-07-01)
- Official text: https://www.dama.org/cpages/body-of-knowledge
- Requirements: 11 (5 facilitated, 6 out-of-scope)
- Browse: https://pryv.github.io/compliance-matrix/#/scope/data-governance

### Data Governance DG-01: Data Governance (framework / accountability)

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: primitive · draft

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv gives you the governance substrate, every datum is owned by a
user (per-user storage isolation), every privileged action is auditable,
and cross-organization sharing is consent-managed (CMC). What Pryv does
NOT give you is the governance *program*: the policies, stewardship
roles, decision rights and oversight cadence. Those are organizational,
start from the QMS templates and the ISO/IEC 38505 Evaluate-Direct-
Monitor model.

**Detail**

ISO/IEC 38505-1 frames governance as accountability for the value, risk
and constraints of data. Pryv's primitives map to the "constraints"
pillar (ownership, access, audit); value and risk decisions remain the
governing body's. The matrix itself is a governance artefact, it makes
"which control covers which obligation" mechanical.

**Evidence**

- qms: qms/pryv/01-policies/quality-policy.md, qms/pryv/01-policies/information-security-policy.md
- primitives: access, audit, CMC, system-streams

### Data Governance DG-04: Data Storage & Operations

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: infrastructure · draft

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv stores each user's data in isolation, lets you choose the storage
engine (PostgreSQL or SQLite) and keep data in-region per core
(residency), and ships backup/restore primitives. Capacity planning,
SLAs, monitoring and the operational runbook are yours (see the QMS
backup-and-recovery + change procedures).

**Evidence**

- primitives: data-residency, backup-restore

### Data Governance DG-05: Data Security

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: high · mode: primitive · draft

**What Pryv does for you**

This is Pryv's strongest data-governance contribution: scoped accesses,
per-stream permissions, privileged-data separation via system streams,
and an audit trail are the enforcement primitives. You still own the
classification-to-control policy (which streams are sensitive, who may
hold which access), Pryv enforces the decisions you encode.

**Detail**

Cross-references the regulation scopes: the same primitives back
gdpr.Art.32, iso-27001 Annex A.5/A.8 access-control rows, and
hipaa-security technical safeguards. Use those rows for the
requirement-level evidence.

**Evidence**

- qms: qms/pryv/01-policies/information-security-policy.md
- primitives: access, permissions, system-streams, audit

### Data Governance DG-06: Data Integration & Interoperability

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: primitive · draft

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv moves data between parties through consented channels, CMC for
controller-to-controller sharing with a consent record, webhooks for
event propagation, and a shared event-type catalogue (data-types) for
semantic interoperability. Pipeline orchestration, transformation
governance and data-contract management remain yours.

**Evidence**

- primitives: CMC, webhooks, data-types

### Data Governance DG-10: Metadata Management

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: storage · draft

**What Pryv does for you**

Streams classify data into a navigable hierarchy, clientData carries
business metadata alongside each access/event, and the data-types
catalogue is a schema registry for event formats. The metadata
*management process* (curation, ownership, glossary upkeep) is yours.

**Evidence**

- primitives: stream, clientData, data-types

### Data Governance DG-02: Data Architecture

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

**What Pryv does for you**

Enterprise data architecture (target-state models, data-flow design
across systems) is the operator's. Pryv is one component within it; its
per-core residency topology is described under DG-04, not here.

### Data Governance DG-03: Data Modeling & Design

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

**What Pryv does for you**

Logical/physical data modelling is an operator design activity. Pryv's
event/stream model is fixed substrate, not a modelling tool.

### Data Governance DG-07: Document & Content Management

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv stores events and attachments, not a document-management system
(records lifecycle, content workflow, e-discovery). Out of software
scope here.

### Data Governance DG-08: Reference & Master Data Management

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

**What Pryv does for you**

MDM (golden records, match/merge, reference-data distribution) is an
operator capability layered above Pryv, not provided by it.

### Data Governance DG-09: Data Warehousing & Business Intelligence

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

**What Pryv does for you**

Analytics warehousing and BI are downstream of Pryv; the operator
builds them from exported/streamed data.

### Data Governance DG-11: Data Quality

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

**What Pryv does for you**

Typed events (data-types) give light structural validation, but a data-
quality program (profiling, rules, remediation, scorecards) is the
operator's. Recorded as out-of-scope rather than overclaiming.


## Digital Healthcare Act (DVG) + DiGA Ordinance (DiGAV) (DiGA)

- Scope id: `diga` (regulation)
- Jurisdiction: Germany
- Version: DiGAV (Digitale-Gesundheitsanwendungen-Verordnung), current consolidated text (2020-04-21)
- Official text: https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/digav/index.html
- Layered on: gdpr, mdr
- Requirements: 24 (4 implemented, 1 configurable, 13 facilitated, 6 out-of-scope)
- Browse: https://pryv.github.io/compliance-matrix/#/scope/diga

### DiGA 4: § 4 Data protection and information security

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: high · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: The digital health application must demonstrate compliance with
requirements on data protection (per GDPR + Bundesdatenschutzgesetz)
and information security (per current state of the art, including
BSI guidelines).

**What Pryv does for you**

The data-protection
half of § 4 derives directly from the GDPR coverage already
authored (see GDPR Art. 5, Art. 25 by-design, Art. 32 security
of processing). The information-security half aligns with the
BSI TR-03161 + BSI C5 baseline; Pryv's primitives (TLS-default
+ AES-256-GCM secrets at rest + audit by default + multi-core
mTLS + MFA + data-residency) carry most of the manufacturer's
"state of the art" claim without additional software work.

**Detail**

For BfArM review, expect to provide:
  - Data-protection concept (Datenschutzkonzept), reuse the
    GDPR rows from this matrix as evidence per concept item.
  - Information-security concept (BSI TR-03161-aligned),
    Pryv's Annex 1 row mappings (below) feed this.
  - Penetration test certificate within 1 year of submission
    for the backend (Pryv) + app sides. Required at listing.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.5, gdpr.Art.25, gdpr.Art.32
- primitives: access, permissions, audit, letsEncrypt-integration, encryption-at-rest-secrets, MFA, data-residency, system-streams, backup-restore

### DiGA 5: § 5 Interoperability

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: The digital health application must support interoperable data
exchange with other systems, in particular electronic patient
records (ePA / TI), based on the semantic and technical standards
named in the BfArM interoperability annex.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv's data-types
schemas (canonical `class/format` JSON Schema) give you a
stable in-platform data model that you can map to FHIR R4 (the
standard BfArM expects). The FHIR-mapping layer is app-side or
implemented as a Pryv data-type extension, not shipped today.
See `proposals/fhir-data-type-mapping.md` if filed, or treat as
a per-app integration concern.

**Detail**

BfArM lists specific HL7 FHIR profiles (KBV / gematik) the device
must consume / produce for ePA interoperability. Pryv's event +
stream model is structurally adequate (events carry typed
content; streams provide hierarchical categorization) but the
mapping is an app-layer transformation today.

**Evidence**

- primitives: event, data-types, stream

### DiGA 6: § 6 Robustness

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: The digital health application must be robust against failure,
interruption and manipulation, with appropriate processes to
address security incidents.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv contributes the
operational baseline: multi-core HA with Raft replication;
cluster-CA mTLS between cores; encrypted bootstrap bundles;
daily-renewed TLS certs; backup + restore; audit-log for
forensic review. The manufacturer's incident-response procedure
(detection, escalation, communication) sits on top of this and
is the regulatory artefact BfArM reviews.

**Evidence**

- primitives: multi-core-mTLS, backup-restore, audit, observability-provider, letsEncrypt-integration

### DiGA 7: § 7 Consumer protection

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Information must be provided to users in a manner that is
comprehensible to laypersons; pricing, intended use, contra-
indications, supported devices + operating systems, data
categories collected, and other minimum elements must be
disclosed in advance.

**What Pryv does for you**

Same artefact set as GDPR
Art. 13 (notice at collection): Pryv stores the text shown to
the user, durably, versioned, per subject, typically on
`access.clientData.privacy_notice` or in a `consent/notice`
event. Drafting the actual text in "lay-comprehensible"
language is the manufacturer's editorial work, not Pryv's.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.13
- primitives: access, clientData, app-web-auth3, event

### DiGA 8: § 8 Patient safety

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: The digital health application must, in its intended use, not
pose unacceptable risks to patient safety. Medical-device
classification + conformity assessment per MDR remain the
manufacturer's process.

**What Pryv does for you**

Patient-safety classification is the manufacturer's regulatory
task per MDR; Pryv has no software role at this layer.
Derives_from points at the MDR Art. 51 (classification) + Art. 52
(conformity) rows where Pryv is similarly out-of-scope.

**Evidence**

- derives from: mdr.Art.51, mdr.Art.52

### DiGA 14: § 14 Positive supply effects (Nutzennachweis)

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: The manufacturer must demonstrate positive supply effects,
medical benefit and/or patient-relevant structural and procedural
improvements, through a comparative study (typically RCT) or,
under specified conditions, real-world evidence.

**What Pryv does for you**

Clinical evidence is the manufacturer's regulatory work. Pryv is
not in scope at the trial design / statistical analysis layer.
For the data-collection substrate during the study, Pryv events
+ audit log are an option, but the regulatory burden of § 14
sits entirely on the manufacturer's clinical team.

### DiGA A1.1.1: Annex 1.1, Data protection, legal basis declared per processing

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: For each processing purpose, the manufacturer must declare the
Art. 6 + (if applicable) Art. 9 GDPR legal basis used.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv pattern:
`access.clientData.legal_basis` captures the Art. 6 basis per
access; for sensitive data,
`clientData.special_category_basis` captures the Art. 9
paragraph. Both travel with the access into the audit log so
the declaration is auditable per processing instance, not just
per system.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.6, gdpr.Art.9
- primitives: access, clientData

### DiGA A1.1.7: Annex 1.1, Data minimisation

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Only data necessary for the intended use shall be processed; data
must be deleted as soon as the purpose is fulfilled.

**What Pryv does for you**

Per-stream permissions are the technical minimisation primitive:
each access carries only the streams + levels needed; the holder
cannot see more than granted. Deletion-when-purpose-fulfilled is
the manufacturer's retention policy, executed via
`system.users.delete` (full erasure) or event/stream-level
deletion (partial).

**Evidence**

- tests: AA01, ACCP
- derives from: gdpr.Art.5
- primitives: permissions, stream

### DiGA A1.2.1: Annex 1.2, Information security, TLS at all interfaces

Coverage: configurable · effort saved: medium · draft

Requirement: All communication interfaces of the digital health application
shall employ Transport Layer Security at current state of the art.

**What Pryv does for you**

TLS is configured, not default: the core terminates it when
`http.ssl.*` is set (the built-in ACME integration issues, renews
and replicates certificates across the cluster when
`letsEncrypt.enabled` is set), otherwise it serves plain HTTP and
your reverse proxy terminates TLS. Inter-core Raft traffic runs
over mTLS with a cluster-private CA once `bin/bootstrap.js` has
written `storages.engines.rqlite.tls` (default plain TCP). The
core sets no TLS version or cipher options of its own, so
"current state of the art" in the core rests on Node.js defaults
(on the Node 24 the image runs: TLS 1.2 floor, TLS 1.3 when the
client supports it); if BfArM expects a TLS 1.3-only or narrower
cipher policy, enforce it at your proxy.

**Evidence**

- tests: ACMEINT, ACMEORCH, CERTUTILS, FORCERENEWIPC
- config keys: http.ssl.keyFile, http.ssl.certFile, letsEncrypt.enabled, storages.engines.rqlite.tls
- derives from: gdpr.Art.32
- primitives: letsEncrypt-integration, multi-core-mTLS

### DiGA A1.2.7: Annex 1.2, Penetration test within 12 months

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: A penetration test performed by an independent third party within
12 months before listing application is required; findings of
"critical" severity must be remediated; "high" findings must have
a mitigation plan.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv supports the
manufacturer's pentest by providing a reproducible deployment
artefact (Docker image), a structured audit log for
verification, and documentation of the security surface. The
test commissioning + remediation cycle is the manufacturer's.
For repeat customers, Pryv-side findings already remediated
upstream reduce repeat test scope.

**Detail**

The 2026 code-level security review of open-pryv.io (fixes in
2.0.0-rc.40 to 2.0.0-rc.51; public report `SECURITY-AUDIT.md`,
published 2026-10-14,
https://github.com/pryv/open-pryv.io/blob/master/SECURITY-AUDIT.md;
`context/code-security-review-2026.md`) does **not**
satisfy this requirement: it was performed by the maintainers of the
code, not by an independent third party, and it reviewed source code,
not your running application. It helps your penetration test: run a
release that carries the fixes before the test, and hand the tester
the report and release notes so known, fixed platform findings are
not re-reported against your listing.

**Evidence**

- primitives: audit
- context notes: code-security-review-2026

### DiGA A1.3.1: Annex 1.3, Interoperability, FHIR R4 export of treatment-relevant data

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: The digital health application must export treatment-relevant
data using HL7 FHIR R4 profiles approved in the BfArM
interoperability annex.

**What Pryv does for you**

Same status as § 5:
Pryv's event model is structurally adequate; the FHIR-mapping
transformation is app-side today. A
"compliance-matrix/proposals/fhir-data-type-mapping.md" entry
tracks the potential Pryv-side mapping primitive for cleaner
downstream coverage.

**Detail**

The implementer's natural extension path is a **FHIR-flavoured
custom event-type catalogue**, a sibling data-model repo
that defines Pryv event types mapping 1-to-1 (or 1-to-many)
to BfArM-approved FHIR resources, published via the standard
`service.eventTypes` extension model (see
`context/custom-event-type-catalogues.md`). The mapping
transformation (Pryv event ↔ FHIR Bundle) still runs
app-side, but the schemas being mapped are first-class
Pryv types validated by the same z-schema pipeline as the
legacy catalogue.

**Evidence**

- derives from: diga.5
- primitives: event, data-types, stream
- context notes: custom-event-type-catalogues

### DiGA A1.6.1: Annex 1.6, Patient safety, usability tested with target group

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Usability of the digital health application shall be tested
against the intended user group prior to listing application;
results documented.

**What Pryv does for you**

Usability testing is the manufacturer's process (UX research +
protocols + documentation). Pryv has no software role at the
usability layer.

### DiGA A1.1.5: Annex 1.1, Data subject rights at the BfArM-specified level

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Mechanisms must be provided to allow data subjects to exercise
their rights under GDPR Art. 15-22 directly within the digital
health application or via a clearly named contact.

**What Pryv does for you**

The personal-token Pryv API gives the data subject direct access
to events, streams, accesses, audit data. Implementer wraps it
in a UI section ("Your data + your rights") inside the DiGA app;
no separate portal needed. Each GDPR Art. 15-22 right has a
single API call behind it.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA01, EGSQ, UZEV, PTU1, USAD
- derives from: gdpr.Art.15, gdpr.Art.16, gdpr.Art.17, gdpr.Art.20
- primitives: access, event, stream, audit

### DiGA A1.2.4: Annex 1.2, Authentication of users and devices

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Strong authentication of users (and where applicable devices)
must be implemented; passwords alone are not sufficient when
sensitive health data is processed.

**What Pryv does for you**

MFA via the `mfa.*` API methods (live by default since
open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.14 with authenticator-app TOTP,
`services.mfa.active`; the legacy `services.mfa.mode` is still
honoured); failed second factors hit a per-account backoff, not a
lockout, since 2.0.0-rc.27 (see HIPAA §164.312(d));
personal-token + access-token model gives separation of user
identity from app identity. The BfArM "strong authentication
where sensitive health data is processed" bar maps to MFA on by
default for DiGA-listed apps.

**Evidence**

- tests: MA15A, MA15C, MA10A, MA11A, MA3A, MA12A
- config keys: services.mfa.mode
- derives from: hipaa-security.164.312(d), iso-27001.A.8.5
- primitives: access, MFA, system-streams

**Planned changes**

- enhancement: Reference WebAuthn plugin meets the BfArM 'strong authentication for sensitive health data' bar without SMS-OTP weakness

### DiGA A1.2.10: Annex 1.2, Logging of security-relevant events

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Security-relevant events must be logged with sufficient detail
to support incident investigation and audit; logs must be
protected against tampering.

**What Pryv does for you**

Per-user audit log records every API method invocation; storage
is SQLite directly (decoupled from data-path engine) so log
integrity is independent of primary engine state. The
audit-event-stream optional channel additionally emits audit
records into the subject's own streams when surface-side
visibility is required.

**Evidence**

- tests: AT01, AT02, AT51, AT61, AT65
- derives from: iso-27001.A.8.15, hipaa-security.164.312(b)
- primitives: audit, audit-event-stream

### DiGA A1.3.6: Annex 1.3, Use of established healthcare data standards

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Where established standards exist for the data domain (FHIR R4,
LOINC, SNOMED CT, ICD-10, etc.), the application shall use them
to encode treatment-relevant data.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv stores whatever event
content the application writes. For LOINC / SNOMED / ICD-10
codings, the implementer encodes the code system + value as
event content fields (typically `event.content.code` +
`event.content.codeSystem`) per the `data-types` schema chosen.
The semantic-standard choice is app-side; Pryv preserves it.

**Evidence**

- primitives: event, data-types, stream

### DiGA A1.4.3: Annex 1.4, Availability and continuity

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: The digital health application must be designed to be available
to users during its specified use periods, with documented
procedures for handling unavailability.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv-side availability:
multi-core HA (cluster topology + Raft replication); TLS
auto-renewal preventing cert-expiry outages; backup-restore for
catastrophic recovery; observability gives uptime metrics. The
application-layer continuity procedures (offline mode,
degraded-service messaging, support channels) are
manufacturer-side.

**Detail**

Since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.47 and 2.0.0-rc.50 the core also
bounds what one client can consume (batch, paging, upload,
socket.io and preview limits; per-address budgets on the
unauthenticated entry points) and replaces a crashing worker after
a growing delay instead of in a tight loop, so a single misbehaving
client is less likely to make the service unavailable for others.
Since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.87, a flood
of password checks no longer stalls a worker's other requests
(a bounded number run at a time, the rest refused with
`Retry-After`), and on PostgreSQL a runaway database statement of an
API request is stopped after a time limit instead of holding its
connection for as long as it takes. From the release after
2.0.0-rc.87, one account, one access or one socket.io connection
can hold only a bounded number of calls and connections at once on
a worker (the extra ones answer `429 too-many-requests`), and
overly nested or oversized call parameters are refused up front.
The same release bounds the depth and size of an account's stream
tree and the stream ids of one event, closes a connection a client
stopped reading after an idle timeout, and caps the mail a caller
can make a core send (registration codes per client address,
verification mails per account, an hourly breaker per core that
keeps password resets apart from registration codes). On a
multi-core platform, each process caches which core hosts a name
and the embedded DNS limits its lookup answers per client network,
so requests or forged DNS queries for random names no longer each
cost a cluster-wide database read.
See `context/rate-limiting-and-dos-protection.md` and iso-27001
A.8.6. An edge layer in front of the cores remains your part.

**Evidence**

- docs: customer-resources/rate-limiting.md
- derives from: iso-27001.A.5.23, mdr.A1.17
- primitives: multi-core-mTLS, letsEncrypt-integration, backup-restore, observability-provider
- context notes: rate-limiting-and-dos-protection

### DiGA A1.5.1: Annex 1.5, Consumer protection, clear pricing + contractual conditions

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: The implementer shall provide users with clear information on
pricing model + contractual conditions (subscription duration,
cancellation terms, renewal mechanics) in advance.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pricing + contract terms are editorial / commercial. No software
role; Pryv stores whatever notice text you present (per A1.1
data-protection notices pattern) but doesn't generate it.

### DiGA A1.5.4: Annex 1.5, Consumer protection, barrier-free access (accessibility)

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: The digital health application shall meet relevant accessibility
requirements (WCAG 2.1 AA equivalent or higher, per BfArM
interpretation), supporting users with disabilities.

**What Pryv does for you**

Accessibility is an app-layer UX concern. Pryv is a backend; the
app's HTML / WAI-ARIA / contrast / keyboard-navigation posture
is the manufacturer's frontend implementation.

### DiGA A1.5.7: Annex 1.5, Consumer protection, clear language + age-appropriate UI

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: User-facing text shall be in clear, plain language; for
applications targeting children or adolescents, the UI shall be
age-appropriate.

**What Pryv does for you**

Plain-language text + age-
appropriate UI are app-layer responsibilities. Pryv contributes
the artefact storage: when different content variants are
served to different age cohorts,
`access.clientData.target_audience` records the variant served,
and `account.clientData.age_verification_method` (per GDPR
Art.8) ties the variant to the verified age. Composition of
the text is editorial.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.8
- primitives: access, clientData, event

### DiGA A1.6.5: Annex 1.6, Patient safety, alarm / escalation logic when applicable

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Where the digital health application generates alarms or
escalation messages (urgent clinical signal, abnormal value
crossing a threshold), the logic shall be documented + validated;
escalation paths shall be tested + reliable.

**What Pryv does for you**

Clinical-alarm logic is the manufacturer's software responsibility
(and falls under MDR Art.61 clinical evaluation + Annex I §17.4
verification). Pryv stores the alarm events; the logic that
produces them is app-side.

### DiGA A1.2.2: Annex 1.2, Documentation of architecture + components

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: awareness · draft

Requirement: Manufacturer shall document the application's architecture
including all components, their role + interactions, and the
security boundary of each.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv's architecture is
publicly documented (open-pryv.io README, AGENTS.md,
component-level READMEs), the BfArM-required architecture
document references Pryv as a sub-system. The app-layer
architecture (services, libraries, network topology) is the
manufacturer's documentation.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27001.A.8.27
- primitives: audit

### DiGA A1.2.3: Annex 1.2, Hardening + secure configuration

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: high · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: The technical platform shall be hardened per current best
practices; configuration shall minimize attack surface
(disabled services, restricted ports, least-privilege defaults).

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv ships secure-by-
default (TLS on, mTLS between cores, no anonymous access path,
system-streams isolating privileged data, at-rest secret
encryption). Operator-side hardening (host OS, firewall,
OS-level least-privilege) layers on top per their hardening
guide.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27001.A.8.9
- primitives: letsEncrypt-integration, multi-core-mTLS, system-streams, encryption-at-rest-secrets

### DiGA A1.2.6: Annex 1.2, Incident response capability

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: Manufacturer shall have documented incident-response procedures,
with detection + escalation + containment + recovery + post-
mortem phases defined.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv contributes detection
(observability anomalies, audit-log patterns) + containment
(accesses.delete revokes implicated tokens) + recovery
(backup-restore + multi-core HA) + post-mortem (audit-log
forensic trail). The manufacturer's IR runbook ties these
primitives together with people + decisions.

**Evidence**

- derives from: hipaa-security.164.308(a)(6)(i), iso-27001.A.5.23
- primitives: audit, observability-provider, access


## General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)

- Scope id: `gdpr` (regulation)
- Jurisdiction: EU + EEA (extraterritorial via Art. 3)
- Version: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (consolidated) (2016-04-27)
- Official text: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02016R0679-20160504
- Requirements: 47 (6 implemented, 3 configurable, 31 facilitated, 7 out-of-scope)
- Browse: https://pryv.github.io/compliance-matrix/#/scope/gdpr

### GDPR Art.1: Subject matter and objectives

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: awareness · draft

Requirement: Regulation lays down rules on the protection of natural persons with
regard to the processing of personal data and rules relating to the
free movement of personal data.

**What Pryv does for you**

GDPR's purpose is to protect
natural persons in how their personal data is processed, while
keeping that data freely movable. Pryv is designed for exactly
that: your subjects own their data, and technical controls enforce
the consent they granted, and the API is open so data can move
without lock-in. The per-article rows below describe how each
obligation maps to the primitives Pryv gives you.

**Detail**

Protection of natural persons (re: processing of their personal data):
  - Subject-centric storage, each of your users has dedicated
    storage; you host but don't commingle subjects.
  - Technical access control, permissions per stream are enforced
    at the API surface; processing only happens within the scope
    the subject granted.
  - Versioned consent record, access + clientData + consent events
    form a tamper-evident chain of what was authorised, when, with
    which contract text.
  - Accountability by construction, audit rows reference the
    specific access version used at processing time.

Free movement of personal data:
  - Open HTTP API, events / streams / accesses consumable without
    vendor SDKs.
  - Canonical event-type schemas, structured JSON with stable
    class/format semantics; portable across deployments.
  - Cross-platform sharing, independent Pryv operators can
    exchange data + consent without shared trust, shared user
    namespace, or federation auth.
  - No vendor lock-in; you can move data + consent contracts
    between operators using the same primitives an end-user would
    use to read them.

A Pryv deployment cannot, on its own, make you GDPR-compliant,
but it gives you the technical substrate on which the per-article
obligations below can be discharged.

**Technical**

Primitives carrying this row:
  - `access` (versioned, immutable per version), see
    `context/access-versioning.md`
  - `permissions` (per-stream, per-level, enforced in
    `open-pryv.io/components/api-server/src/methods/`)
  - `audit` (per-API-call rows tagged with `accessId` + `accessSerial`)
  - `data-types` (canonical class/format schemas at
    `https://raw.github.com/pryv/data-types/master/dist/event-types.json`)
  - `CMC` plugin (`open-pryv.io/components/cmc/`, shipped 2.0.0-pre.3)

**Evidence**

- primitives: access, permissions, stream, audit, data-types, CMC
- context notes: access-versioning

### GDPR Art.2: Material scope

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: awareness · draft

Requirement: Applies to the processing of personal data wholly or partly by
automated means and to the processing other than by automated means
of personal data which form part of a filing system.

**What Pryv does for you**

Your Pryv deployment is
fully inside Article 2's material scope. Every event you store
and every API call your apps make is automated processing
covered by GDPR. Pryv does not exempt you from any per-article
obligation; it gives you the technical primitives that make
those obligations addressable (see Art.5+). Branch 2 (non-
automated processing inside a "filing system", structured
paper records) doesn't surface at the Pryv layer; your own
paper records, if any, are outside the software boundary.

**Detail**

GDPR Art.4(6) defines "filing system" as any structured set of
personal data accessible by specific criteria, alphabetised
customer cards, dated patient folders, indexed application forms.
Random unstructured paper or spoken-only data is not in scope.

Pryv is fully digital, so branch 1 always applies; branch 2 is moot.
If you also keep paper records as part of the same business process,
those fall under branch 2 but as a separate process you manage
outside Pryv.

**Evidence**

- primitives: access, event, audit

### GDPR Art.3: Territorial scope

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: Applies to processing in the context of an establishment in the
Union, or where processing relates to data subjects in the Union.

**What Pryv does for you**

Whether GDPR applies
to your Pryv deployment depends on where you're established and
where your data subjects are, not on the software. Pryv is
self-hosted, so you control data residency directly: the multi-
hosting feature lets you choose which jurisdiction each core
runs in, and either let end-users pick their hosting at
registration or auto-route them by your policy. If any of your
subjects are in the EU/EEA, GDPR applies to your deployment in
full.

**Detail**

Pryv supports a single logical platform spanning multiple hostings
(different countries / cloud regions / on-premise). Two routing
policies you can apply:

- **End-user choice**: your registration UI presents the available
  hostings (via `auth.hostings`); user picks. Useful for consumer
  apps where subjects assert their own residency preference.
- **Operator / regulatory routing**: your app auto-routes based on
  the subject's jurisdiction or contract terms (e.g., EU subjects →
  EU hosting; French health data → HDS-certified French hosting).

The chosen hosting binds the user's data to that core permanently.
`system.users.get` exposes the per-user hosting so you can surface
it in the app ("your data is stored in <region>").

Note: even with EU-only hosting, if you have a non-EU establishment
offering services to EU subjects, Art.3(2) still pulls you into
GDPR.

**Evidence**

- primitives: data-residency

### GDPR Art.4: Definitions

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: awareness · draft

Requirement: Defines key terms: personal data, processing, controller, processor,
consent, profiling, pseudonymisation, etc.

**What Pryv does for you**

Article 4 defines GDPR
vocabulary. Pryv's primitives map cleanly to most of these
terms, easier for you to point auditors at concrete artefacts
rather than abstract concepts.

**Detail**

Approximate mapping of key GDPR terms to Pryv primitives:

| GDPR term | Pryv primitive |
|---|---|
| personal data | `event` content + attachments on a user's account |
| data subject | the user (account owner) |
| controller | typically you, the implementer |
| processor | the Pryv operator (when distinct from you) |
| recipient | a counterparty holding an `access` to the data |
| third party | another deployment / app accessing via shared/app `access` |
| consent | app/shared `access` with `permissions` + `clientData` carrying the contract (see Art.7) |
| processing | any API call on `events.*` / `streams.*` / `accesses.*` (audit-recorded) |
| filing system | N/A, Pryv is fully automated |
| personal data breach | event/audit anomaly + post-mortem (see Art.33) |
| pseudonymisation | `accesses.create {randomAlias:true}` (platform-unique routable alias hides the username per access from its holder; since 2.0.0-rc.69 the token is accepted under its alias only, so a holder who guesses the username cannot confirm it with the token, see Art.32) + external ids (a third-party record id held only as a value the caller blinds with its own key, open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.58) + system-streams + custom event-type design |
| profiling | application-side concern (out for Pryv) |
| restriction of processing | scope-down via `accesses.update` (see Art.18) |

The controller/processor distinction is contractual; you assign
the roles. Pryv lets you record the assignment explicitly in
`access.clientData` if you want it traceable.

**Evidence**

- primitives: access, permissions, stream, event, system-streams, randomAlias, external-id-index

### GDPR Art.5: Principles relating to processing of personal data

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high

Requirement: Lawfulness, fairness, transparency; purpose limitation; data
minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and
confidentiality (security); accountability.

**What Pryv does for you**

Several Art.5 principles are technically enforced for you by Pryv
rather than left to policy: purpose limitation (per-stream
permissions), accountability (audit chain to the consent state),
accuracy (schema validation at ingest; the prior value of a
corrected event is kept when you turn on event history with
`versioning.forceKeepHistory: true`, off by default). Lawfulness,
fairness and transparency
stay on your shoulders; Pryv stores the notice/consent text you
present but doesn't generate it for you.

**Detail**

Per-principle breakdown, what Pryv does for you, what you do:

- Lawfulness, fairness, transparency (§1(a)), DOCUMENTED. You
  write the notice and present it; Pryv carries the text in
  `access.clientData` or a `consent/request-cmc` event so the
  same text is recoverable later.
- Purpose limitation (§1(b)), IMPLEMENTED. `permissions` per
  stream technically restrict reads/writes to the granted scope;
  an app cannot access streams outside its granted permissions.
- Data minimisation (§1(c)), FACILITATED. Permissions + stream
  design let apps see only what's in their scope; the rest is
  invisible to them.
- Accuracy (§1(d)), FACILITATED + IMPLEMENTER-OWNED.
  Pryv enforces **structural** accuracy at ingest: every
  `events.create` and `events.update` validates against the
  declared event-type's JSON Schema (ajv-draft-04 via
  `components/utils/src/jsonValidator.ts`), rejecting
  out-of-shape or out-of-range payloads with HTTP 400.
  Numerical bounds (`minimum`/`maximum`), string patterns,
  and length limits are expressible per type, the HDS
  data-model exemplar declares 28 `minimum`/23 `maximum`
  constraints across health-data types. The built-in
  catalogue uses bounds sparingly (operator opts into
  strictness by extending via `service.eventTypes` URL,
  Q14 pattern). **Semantic** accuracy, "is this medication
  right for THIS patient?", is out of scope by design;
  the implementer's app layer carries the clinical /
  domain context Pryv intentionally doesn't see.
  `events.update` rectifies events (Art.16). The prior
  value is kept, and returned by `GET
  /events/:id?includeHistory=true`, only on a deployment
  with `versioning.forceKeepHistory: true` (default
  `false`: the update overwrites it); set it if your
  accuracy trail must show the value before correction.
  The audit log records who rectified which event and when
  either way, not the prior value (see
  `context/event-history.md`). Full split
  in `context/data-accuracy-structural-vs-semantic.md`.
- Storage limitation (§1(e)), CONFIGURABLE for whole accounts
  (account auto-deletion) + VOLUNTARILY MISSING and
  OPERATOR-OWNED for event-level and stream-level retention +
  CONFIGURABLE at the erasure-mechanics layer. Pryv exposes no
  TTL / auto-delete / scheduler primitive for events and
  streams (whole accounts are covered by account auto-deletion
  since 2.0.0-rc.66, below): event-level and stream-level
  automatic retention is the operator's external job, composing
  `events.get toTime=<cutoff>` + `events.delete` (two-stage)
  + `streams.delete` + `auth.delete` + the audit log as
  inactivity oracle. Every retention deletion is captured
  by the audit log automatically (Q9 audit-by-construction).
  Engine-dependent backup-tail considerations apply (see
  Art.17). Full pattern + cron-job recipe + audit-trace
  treatment + "why not built-in" rationale in
  `context/data-retention-operator-owned.md`. One narrow
  built-in purge exists since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.56: the
  deletion records of accesses, opt-in with
  `accesses.deletionRecords.retentionDays` (default 0, kept
  until the account is deleted).

  Account auto-deletion, since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.66
  (`8521c8d5`): an account is deleted at a date its holder
  picks, or after a period without use of its personal
  accesses (a sign-in counts, `[LGLU3]`; a delegate's own token
  included, shared accesses never, `[ACAC1]`, `[ACAC2]`,
  `[ACAC7]`; since 2.0.0-rc.81 app accesses count only with
  `account.autoDeletion.inactivity.countAppUse`, default false,
  `[ACST20]`). Two sources: the holder's own schedule (their
  erasure request, see Art.17), or your inactivity preset
  (`account.autoDeletion.inactivity.defaultDays`, default none).
  A preset is your storage-limitation rule: state the period and
  what counts as use in your privacy notice (Art.13 §2(a)).
  Reminder mails before the deletion (60, 30, 7 and 1 days by
  default, `[ACXP3]`), no deletion less than 7 days
  after the first notice actually sent (`[ACXP8]`); a preset
  applies only to plain accounts with an email address on a core
  that sends mail (`[ACST14]`, `[ADSW9]`), and its clock starts
  the day it first applies, so turning one on never deletes
  dormant accounts by surprise (`[ACXP2]`, `[ACXP10]`); a dry run
  shows the numbers first (`[ADSW13]`). Inactivity needs
  `accessTracking.isActive`: a preset without it refuses the
  boot (`[CVAD3]`), and a holder's inactivity schedule is
  suspended, never erased, while tracking is off (`[ACXP19]`).
  The erasure is `auth.delete`'s, guards included (`[ADSW8]`).
  An exception for one account is yours to grant: since the
  release after open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.87 your support can
  restart a pending preset schedule from now, with its full
  period and reminders (a holder who cannot sign in in time),
  reasoned, mailed to the holder and recorded in the account's
  trail (`POST /system/admin/auto-deletion/clear`, see Art.17)
  `[ADCL3]`.
  Event-level and stream-level retention stays your retention
  job. See `context/data-retention-operator-owned.md`,
  "Account-level auto-deletion", and the operator page
  `customer-resources/account-auto-deletion`.

  Leftovers of unfinished registrations (the release after
  open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.87; merged, unreleased at this walk). A
  registration that fails, or whose process dies midway, can
  leave personal data that no finished account owns: account
  fields (the email included) under an id the users index lacks,
  an indexed account with no password, or an email still
  reserved on the platform for a name that never got its
  account. From that release a failed registration's
  compensation removes its account fields on PostgreSQL too
  (earlier, a failed first registration in a freshly started
  worker kept them, email included, with no owner) `[URB2]`. For
  what an earlier failure or a crash left, run
  `bin/reconcile-user-cores.js --registrations` on each core. It
  only reports unless given `--apply`; it clears an orphan id
  (PostgreSQL) only when the id holds account fields alone, no
  erasure record, and is older than `--grace` (default 24 hours)
  `[RCRG1]`, `[RCRG2]`; it erases an indexed account with no
  password (both engines) only when you name it with `--user-id`
  and it still passes every check, through the account
  deletion's erasure, resumable through the record of the
  erasure in progress `[RCRG3]`, `[RCRG5]`, keeping the platform rows of a
  name another core holds now `[MCUR2]`; an empty users index
  facing account rows is refused (exit 3) `[RCRG7]`. The default
  username pass of the same tool now releases the email and
  other unique values a stale name held, before its routing row
  `[RCRG6]`, `[MCUR1]`. Run both as a dry run first: a name whose
  account is missing for another reason (a partly lost users
  index) loses its reserved email too. The pass's own log lines
  carry ids and counts, never an email or field value; the
  account erasure it runs logs the account name, as every
  account erasure does.
  Procedure: open-pryv.io `INSTALL.md`, "Unfinished
  registrations".
- Data minimisation, planned with the account transfer (the
  release after the deletion one; implemented, not released): a
  holder may name a beneficiary who receives control of the
  account at the deadline. Only the beneficiary's email is
  required; a name and date of birth are optional, kept
  encrypted, unreadable before the transfer starts, and erased
  with the transfer (§1(c)).
- Integrity & confidentiality (§1(f)), covered separately at Art.32.
- Accountability (§2), IMPLEMENTED. Every API call audited with
  the access reference + version; access carries the consent state
  at that version → end-to-end accountability chain you can point
  auditors at.

  Proof of erasure (the release after open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.87,
  `83e14c94`). Every account erasure, whoever decided it, leaves
  one durable record in the platform database, the erasure
  ledger: keyed hashes of the user id and username, when the
  erasure started and ended, its trigger, the core, the steps
  done; no username, email or account data `[ERLG3]`, `[ERLG4]`.
  An erasure never looks finished without it `[ERLG6]`. You
  answer "was this account erased, and when?" with
  `POST /system/admin/erasures/lookup` or `bin/erasures.js
  --check`, and list erasures since a date with
  `GET /system/admin/erasures` `[ERLA2]`, `[ERLA4]`. Records are
  kept 1825 days by default
  (`accountErasure.ledger.retentionDays`, `0` keeps them; the
  shortest value set on any core applies to all) `[ERLT4]`. The
  lookup counts the records under another key it cannot match
  (`otherKeyRecords`): keep the ledger key across admin-key
  rotations or the older proof can no longer be found by id or
  name `[ERLA6]`. The hashes are pseudonymous personal data while
  the key exists: name the ledger in your record of processing
  (Art.30). See Art.17, "Proof of erasure and restores".

**Technical**

- Purpose limitation: enforcement in
  `open-pryv.io/components/api-server/src/methods/` permission-checks.
- Accountability: audit row schema includes
  `(accessId, accessSerial)`; access-version snapshot includes
  `clientData` (consent state), see `context/access-versioning.md`.

**Evidence**

- tests: GLHP, UZEV, ACXP2, ACXP3, ACXP8, ACXP10, ACXP19, ACAC1, ACAC2, ACAC7, ADSW8, ADSW9, ADSW13, ACST14, LGLU3, CVAD3, URB2, RCRG1, RCRG2, RCRG3, RCRG5, RCRG6, RCRG7, MCUR1, MCUR2, ERLG3, ERLG4, ERLG6, ERLA2, ERLA4, ERLA6, ERLT4, ADCL3
- specs: EVENT.BASE, STREAM.BASE
- docs: customer-resources/account-auto-deletion.md
- config keys: account.autoDeletion.inactivity.defaultDays, account.autoDeletion.inactivity.countAppUse, account.autoDeletion.userOverride, account.autoDeletion.allowUserOptOut, account.autoDeletion.reminders.leadDays, account.autoDeletion.reminders.minNoticeDays, account.autoDeletion.dryRun, accessTracking.isActive, accountErasure.ledger.enabled, accountErasure.ledger.retentionDays
- primitives: access, permissions, clientData, stream, audit, account-auto-deletion
- samples: scheduled-retention-job
- context notes: event-history, data-accuracy-structural-vs-semantic, data-retention-operator-owned, access-versioning

**Planned changes**

- feature: Account transfer to a beneficiary (release after the deletion one): §1(c) minimisation of the beneficiary's data (email required; name and date of birth optional, encrypted, erased with the transfer)

### GDPR Art.6: Lawfulness of processing

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Processing lawful only if at least one of six bases applies (consent,
contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public interest,
legitimate interests). §4, further processing for a purpose other
than the original is lawful only if compatible per the five-factor
test OR a fresh lawful basis applies.

**What Pryv does for you**

You decide which Art.6 basis
you're relying on for each processing activity. Pryv doesn't
impose or check the basis. You can record your chosen basis in
`access.clientData.lawful_basis` so it travels alongside the
technical authorization and lives in the audit trail, handy
when an auditor asks "under what basis was this access made?".
For Art.6(4) further processing (purpose pivot), Pryv exposes
four composable patterns + a clear decision rule for when the
purpose pivot demands fresh consent vs. an in-place update,
see detail.

**Detail**

Recording the basis on the access gives you a durable, versioned
artefact tying the basis to the specific processing scope it
justifies. Determination of which basis applies remains your
responsibility, Pryv neither enforces nor refuses on the basis
claim.

**§4, further processing (purpose pivot).** Four composable
patterns; choose per the compatibility-vs-fresh-consent
decision rule below.

**Pattern A, Mint a new access for the new purpose.** The
cleanest fit when the new purpose is **outside** the original
OR is not covered by a fresh override-by-law basis (Art.6(4)(a)
compatibility test fails). The subject sees a fresh auth flow;
`app-web-auth3` presents the new notice + new purpose explicitly;
the new access carries `clientData.purpose: <new>` +
`clientData.lawful_basis: <fresh>`. Old access keeps operating
for its original purpose (or is revoked separately if
withdrawn). This pattern is the **mandatory** path when the
compatibility test fails, fresh consent is required.

**Pattern B, Update existing access** (`accesses.update`).
Suitable when the purpose change is narrow / compatible (e.g.,
scope-down or compatible expansion). The pre-mutation
`permissions` + `clientData` snapshot into a history row
automatically (see `context/access-versioning.md`), preserving
the purpose-history chain end-to-end. The bumped `accessSerial`
threads through the audit log so post-pivot rows correctly
attribute to the new purpose state.

**Pattern C, Separate compatibility-assessment event.** When
the operator wants the Art.6(4) 5-factor analysis itself
recorded as a first-class artefact, write a
`compliance/compatibility-assessments/<id>` event on a
dedicated stream (operator-authored format via Q14 custom
catalogue) capturing the §6(4)(a)-(e) reasoning + the affected
data scope + the decision outcome. The relevant access(es)
then reference it via
`clientData.compatibility_assessment_event_id`. This pattern
composes with A or B (the assessment artefact justifies the
pattern choice).

**Pattern D, Sub-access derivation from an `app` access**
(`createdBy` mechanism, see `context/workforce-access-patterns.md`
Pattern 2). When the operator's app holds an `app`-type access
with broad scope; it can mint per-purpose **sub-accesses**,
each carrying its own narrower `permissions[]` +
`clientData.purpose`: and the audit log records each
sub-access's id independently, **feeding purpose-driven access
matching into the audit trail at query time** (`audit.get` →
group by `accessId` → distinct purposes touched). Especially
clean when the same app legitimately operates under multiple
compatible-purpose facets, each facet gets its own sub-access,
so per-purpose disclosure accounting (Art.30 / §164.528)
reconstructs from the audit log without operator-side
bookkeeping.

**Decision rule** (operator-side):

1. New purpose is **inside** the original purpose's scope (a
   compatible refinement / narrowing) → **Pattern B** update
   existing access. No fresh consent. Update notice if material.
2. New purpose is **alongside** the original (compatible
   expansion, same app, multiple facets) → **Pattern D**
   sub-access mint, OR **Pattern A** new access. No fresh
   consent required if compatibility test passes;
   transparency-notice update may be required under Art.13(3).
3. New purpose is **outside** the original AND not covered by
   a fresh override-by-law basis (Art.6(1)(c)/(d)/(e)) →
   **Pattern A** mint new access + force fresh consent. The
   subject's positive opt-in is mandatory under Art.6(4) when
   compatibility fails. App-web-auth3's grant flow IS the
   re-prompt mechanism.
4. In **any** case where the 5-factor compatibility analysis
   was non-trivial → **Pattern C** separate compatibility-
   assessment event for audit-defensibility.

**Re-prompt surface (§4 fallback):** Pryv has no built-in
"notice changed → automatically re-prompt subject" workflow.
The operator's app layer triggers re-auth by minting a new
access (Pattern A), `app-web-auth3` presents the updated
notice; the subject's positive consent IS the fresh-basis
capture. For revocation of the old access alongside the
new mint, `accesses.delete` is the standard path (Q19 / Q28
mechanism family).

**clientData convention extension** for §4 purpose pivots:
`compatibility_assessment_event_id` + `purpose_change_basis`
(`compatible_purpose` / `new_consent` / `new_legal_obligation`
/ `new_legitimate_interest`) + `previous_purpose` (the pivot
record). See `context/client-data-conventions.md`.

**Planned, implemented and not released: account transfer to a
beneficiary** (the release after account auto-deletion). A
holder may name one person who receives control of the account
at its deadline; the platform then stores that person's email
and, if the holder gives them, their name and date of birth.
The beneficiary is not the one who gave the data, so the basis
is yours to establish as operator. The reading recorded in
`context/data-retention-operator-owned.md` ("Planned: transfer
to a beneficiary") is Art.6(1)(f): the holder's legitimate
interest in arranging what happens to their own account, and
yours in carrying out that instruction, balanced by
minimisation (only the email required), encryption at rest, no
read path before the transfer starts, and erasure with the
transfer. Unconfirmed: it needs your DPO's or counsel's reading
before you offer the transfer.

**Evidence**

- primitives: access, clientData, audit, event
- context notes: access-versioning, workforce-access-patterns, client-data-conventions, data-retention-operator-owned

**Planned changes**

- feature: Account transfer to a beneficiary (implemented, not released): the platform stores a third party's email, and optionally name and date of birth, on the holder's instruction; the operator needs a basis for that processing

### GDPR Art.7: Conditions for consent

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high

Requirement: Where processing is based on consent, controller must be able to
demonstrate consent. Request must be in intelligible form,
withdrawable.

**What Pryv does for you**

The access Pryv mints when your user grants permission IS your
durable consent record, versioned permissions + clientData
together prove what was authorised, with what text, at what time.
Withdrawal is a single API call. For cross-account sharing, the
`consent/*` events carry the negotiation state transitions. The
access keeps every previous version; an event keeps its previous
versions only on a deployment with
`versioning.forceKeepHistory: true` (off by default), and the
server-written parts of the accept event (who approved, the
withdrawal) cannot be changed by any client.

**Detail**

Demonstrability (§1), `accesses.get ?includeHistory=true` returns
the full version chain; each version preserves the `permissions`
granted and the `clientData` (which can carry the consent contract
text) at that point in time. For cross-account flows, the original
`consent/request-cmc` event on the requester's account holds the
localised consent text presented.

What a grant covers is a set of streams, and a release can widen
what a stream carries. Since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.44, an
access holding a grant on the account email
stream (`:system:email`, "Read Email") can also request, by type,
a read-only, server-derived `verification/email` event (whether
the primary address was proved, by which method, and when),
including apps granted it before that release, without new consent. A read
without that type returns the address only, as before. Other addresses of the
account are never returned. If the consent text you present should
name this, rename the email field's `name` in
`custom.systemStreams`.

Withdrawal (§3), `accesses.delete` (full revoke) or `accesses.update`
with narrower `permissions` (scope-down). Both bump the access
serial + snapshot the pre-mutation state. Cross-account:
`consent/revoke-cmc` triggers symmetric teardown on both sides
via the CMC plugin. Since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.53 every CMC and
delegation teardown (a `consent/revoke-cmc` revoke, a revocation
received from the counterparty, an accept rolled back, a
delegation detach, the teardown at account deletion) is the
`accesses.delete` deletion: the data grant is marked deleted and
stays readable by name (never by token) with `includeDeletions`,
its webhooks are deleted and its alias released `[GA30]`. Before
that release these paths removed the access row outright, so for
a withdrawal made then the record you demonstrate is the
`consent/*` events (the accept on the subject's account, the
request on the requester's) plus the audit trail, not the access
version chain. When the offer made the grant delegable
(`request.accessType: 'app'`), every withdrawal path also deletes
the accesses the requester derived from it, since open-pryv.io
2.0.0-rc.52 (`96af58ad`) `[MAAC]`, `[CMCHS-APPGRANT]`, `[GA24]`;
on earlier releases they stayed valid until their own expiry, and
`bin/access-scope-audit.js` lists any left behind. The
withdrawal is effective on the withdrawing account at once; the
notice to the counterparty, when it cannot be reached, is queued
and re-sent by the retry loop since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.53
(eight re-sends over about 27 hours, then marked failed for the
operator, https://github.com/pryv/open-pryv.io/issues/157)
`[HR25]`, `[DH25]`, `[RQ20]`, `[RQ21]`, `[RQ22]`, `[RQ23]`, and a
late notice never tears down a relationship the parties
re-established meanwhile `[CIR26]`, `[CIR27]`. Not re-sent: the
notices of an account being deleted (no account is left to hold
them), and any notice while `cmc.retryLoop.enabled` is `false`.
Nor, since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.56, a notice to an address Pryv
refuses to call (loopback, private or reserved, unless listed in
`cmc.allowedPrivateHosts`; see Art.32): it is tried once and
marked failed at once `[HR41]`, `[RQ33]`. The same release has
the retry loop act only on records the server wrote into its
queue `[RQ32]`. The person's own accept event also records the
end itself, whatever ended the consent: `content.withdrawal = { at, by,
accessId, revokeEventId? }`, with `by: 'accesses.delete'` (the
