### ISO 27001 A.5.25: A.5.25 Assessment and decision on information security events

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: The organization shall assess information security events and
decide if they are to be categorized as information security
incidents.

**What Pryv does for you**

Event-vs-incident
classification is operator decision. Pryv-side data (audit row
patterns, observability anomalies) feeds the assessment but the
categorization rule is operator policy.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27001.A.5.24
- primitives: audit, observability-provider

### ISO 27001 A.5.30: A.5.30 ICT readiness for business continuity

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: ICT readiness shall be planned, implemented, maintained and
tested based on business continuity objectives and ICT
continuity requirements.

**What Pryv does for you**

ICT-readiness Pryv
inheritance: multi-core HA + backup-restore + cluster-replicated
TLS certificates. The business-continuity objectives + testing
cadence are operator policy.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27001.A.8.14, hipaa-security.164.308(a)(7)(ii)(B)
- primitives: multi-core-mTLS, backup-restore, letsEncrypt-integration


## ISO/IEC 27701, Extension to ISO/IEC 27001 for Privacy Information Management (ISO 27701)

- Scope id: `iso-27701` (standard)
- Jurisdiction: International (ISO/IEC)
- Version: ISO/IEC 27701:2019 (2019-08-01)
- Official text: https://www.iso.org/standard/71670
- Layered on: iso-27001
- Requirements: 26 (11 implemented, 2 configurable, 10 facilitated, 3 out-of-scope)
- Browse: https://pryv.github.io/compliance-matrix/#/scope/iso-27701

### ISO 27701 5: Clause 5 PIMS-specific requirements extending ISO 27001

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: awareness · draft

Requirement: Organization shall apply the requirements of ISO/IEC 27001
treating privacy as an information-security concern; PII
controllers and processors apply Annex A and/or B respectively.

**What Pryv does for you**

27701 extends the 27001
ISMS to cover PII handling specifically. Pryv contribution is
the same primitive set surfaced in the iso-27001 rows + the
GDPR rows; 27701 simply combines them under the privacy-
information-management label. The organization's PIMS-specific
risk treatment and statement of applicability sit on top.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27001.6.1.2
- primitives: access, audit

### ISO 27701 A.7.2.1: A.7.2.1 Identify and document purpose

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Organization shall identify and document the specific purposes
for which PII will be processed.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv pattern:
`access.clientData.purpose` records the per-access purpose at
grant time, durable + auditable. The vocabulary of purposes
(the organization's documented PIMS catalogue) is the operator's
editorial work; Pryv carries each instance forward.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.5
- primitives: access, clientData

### ISO 27701 A.7.2.2: A.7.2.2 Identify lawful basis

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Organization shall determine, document, and comply with the
relevant lawful basis for processing of PII.

**What Pryv does for you**

`access.clientData.lawful_basis`
records the determined basis (consent, contract, legal
obligation, etc.); for special-category PII,
`clientData.special_category_basis` records the GDPR Art. 9
paragraph or equivalent. Both travel with the access into the
audit chain.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.6, gdpr.Art.9
- primitives: access, clientData

### ISO 27701 A.7.3.1: A.7.3.1 Determining and fulfilling obligations to PII principals

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Organization shall determine and document its legal, regulatory,
and business obligations to PII principals related to the
processing of their PII.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv ships the technical fulfilment of the PII-principal-rights
obligations: the subject (PII principal) holding a personal
token reads everything via the standard API. The organization's
response procedure (timeline, identity verification, content of
response) is the policy half; Pryv responds in milliseconds.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA01, EGSQ, UZEV
- specs: EVENT.BASE, STREAM.BASE
- derives from: gdpr.Art.12, gdpr.Art.15
- primitives: access, stream, event, audit, data-types

### ISO 27701 A.7.3.4: A.7.3.4 Providing mechanism to modify or withdraw consent

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Organization shall provide a mechanism for PII principals to
modify or withdraw their consent.

**What Pryv does for you**

Withdrawal = `accesses.delete`; modification = `accesses.update`
with new permissions / clientData. Both are versioned and
auditable; the prior consent state is preserved for §7
demonstrability. Cross-account (CMC) consent withdrawal uses
`consent/revoke-cmc` for symmetric teardown, and since
open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.36 the principal's own
accept event records each withdrawal, whichever party and path
ended it (`content.withdrawal`, server-owned, never overwritten)
`[CN58]`, `[CN59]`, `[CN60]`. See
`context/cmc-consent-primitives.md`.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA02, ACCP, CN58, CN59, CN60
- derives from: gdpr.Art.7
- primitives: access, permissions, CMC
- context notes: cmc-consent-primitives

### ISO 27701 A.7.4.1: A.7.4.1 Limit collection

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Organization shall limit the collection of PII to the minimum
relevant, proportionate and necessary for the identified
purposes.

**What Pryv does for you**

Per-stream permissions are the technical minimisation control;
stream topology design determines the granularity. The operator's
decision of which streams a given app's access should touch IS
the limit-collection enforcement, expressed in `permissions[]`.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA01, ACCP
- derives from: gdpr.Art.5
- primitives: access, permissions, stream

### ISO 27701 A.7.4.7: A.7.4.7 Records of PII processing

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Organization shall determine and securely maintain the necessary
records in support of its obligations for the processing of PII.

**What Pryv does for you**

Same artefact set as GDPR Art. 30: access + clientData + audit +
CMC + data-residency primitives constitute the records-of-
processing register (purpose, basis, recipients, transfers,
retention, security). Derivable per PII-principal per time
window.

**Evidence**

- tests: UZEV, TJ8S, AA01
- docs: customer-resources/audit-setup.md, guides/audit-logs.md
- derives from: gdpr.Art.30
- primitives: access, clientData, audit, CMC, data-residency

### ISO 27701 B.8.4.1: B.8.4.1, Confidentiality

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: Persons under the processor's authority who have access to PII
shall be subject to a confidentiality commitment.

**What Pryv does for you**

The confidentiality commitment
is an organizational artefact (employment agreements, contractor
NDAs). Pryv's contribution: the audit log gives per-person
accountability so the commitment is enforceable in practice
(any breach is attributable to an access tied to a person).

**Evidence**

- primitives: access, permissions, audit

### ISO 27701 B.8.5.4: B.8.5.4, Records related to processing PII

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Processor shall determine and maintain necessary records related
to the processing of PII to support compliance with applicable
obligations.

**What Pryv does for you**

When Pryv operates as processor (i.e., when the implementer is
the controller and the Pryv operator is distinct), the same
audit chain documented under iso-27001 A.8.15 + iso-27701 A.7.4.7
satisfies the processor-side records-of-processing requirement.
The processor's specific obligations (subprocessor list, transfer
register) are operator-side artefacts.

**Evidence**

- tests: AT01, AT51, AT61
- derives from: iso-27701.A.7.4.7
- primitives: audit, access

### ISO 27701 A.7.4.2: A.7.4.2 Limit processing

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Organization shall limit the processing of PII to that which is
adequate, relevant and necessary for the identified purposes.

**What Pryv does for you**

Same primitive as A.7.4.1 limit collection, per-stream
permissions are the technical limit on what processing each
access can perform. The "adequate / relevant / necessary"
assessment per purpose is the controller's; the technical
enforcement is permission-shaped.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA01, ACCP
- derives from: iso-27701.A.7.4.1, gdpr.Art.5
- primitives: access, permissions, stream

### ISO 27701 A.7.4.3: A.7.4.3 Accuracy and quality

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Organization shall ensure and document that PII is as accurate,
complete and up-to-date as is necessary for the purposes for
which it is processed throughout the lifecycle of the PII.

**What Pryv does for you**

`events.update` rectifies events (matching GDPR Art.16 mechanics),
and the audit log records who rectified which event and when. For
"throughout the lifecycle" proof of the values themselves, the
event version chain is the artefact, and it exists only on a
deployment with `versioning.forceKeepHistory: true` (off by
default; see `context/event-history.md`). The accuracy
determination + correction workflow is the controller's.

**Evidence**

- tests: PTU1
- derives from: gdpr.Art.5, gdpr.Art.16
- primitives: event
- context notes: event-history

### ISO 27701 A.7.4.5: A.7.4.5 PII de-identification and deletion at end of processing

Coverage: configurable · effort saved: medium · draft

Requirement: Organization shall either delete PII or render it in a form which
does not permit identification or re-identification of PII
principals, as soon as the original PII is no longer necessary
for the identified purpose(s).

**What Pryv does for you**

Per-user deletion via `system.users.delete` (engine-dependent
backup behaviour, same notes as GDPR Art. 17). Per-event /
per-stream deletion lives alongside for partial-deletion needs.
De-identification (Safe Harbor / Expert Determination methods) is
an application-layer transformation; Pryv stores the result.
"**Soon as the original PII is no longer necessary**" is the
operator's scheduled-retention obligation for records; Pryv
ships no TTL primitive for events and streams (whole accounts:
account auto-deletion since 2.0.0-rc.66, see detail); the
operator composes `events.get toTime=` + `events.delete` +
audit-log inactivity oracle in an external
retention job (`context/data-retention-operator-owned.md`).
`accesses.create {randomAlias:true}` reduces identification at
the access layer while processing continues: a platform-unique
routable alias replaces the username on that access, so what the
server returns to a counterparty holding it does not name the
principal nor match it against another access. It is not an
end-of-processing de-identification of the PII (the data stays
linked to the account). Since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.69 the token
is accepted under its alias only, so a counterparty who guesses
the username cannot confirm it with the token (earlier releases
accepted it under every name of the account). At the end of
processing, deletion stays the mechanism.

**Detail**

Account auto-deletion, since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.66
(`8521c8d5`, see gdpr.Art.5 §1(e)). For whole accounts, "no
longer necessary" is enforceable by configuration: your
inactivity preset (`account.autoDeletion.inactivity.defaultDays`,
default none) deletes plain accounts with an email address
(`[ACST14]`) after that many days without use of their personal
accesses (app accesses too only with
`account.autoDeletion.inactivity.countAppUse`, since
2.0.0-rc.81, `[ACST20]`), its clock starting the day it first applies
(`[ACXP2]`), after reminder mails (`[ACXP3]`) and at least 7 days
after the first notice (`[ACXP8]`); the PII principal may also
schedule their own account's deletion at a date or after a
period, where self-deletion is allowed (`[ACST10]`). The deletion
is `system.users.delete`'s, guards included (`[ADSW8]`).
Per-record retention and de-identification stay as above.

**Evidence**

- tests: USAD, ACXP2, ACXP3, ACXP8, ACST10, ACST14, ADSW8
- docs: customer-resources/account-auto-deletion.md
- config keys: storages.userAccountStorage.engine, user-account.delete, account.autoDeletion.inactivity.defaultDays, account.autoDeletion.reminders.minNoticeDays
- derives from: gdpr.Art.17, gdpr.Art.4, hipaa-security.164.310, hipaa-privacy.164.514, ccpa.1798.105
- primitives: event, stream, backup-restore, randomAlias, account-auto-deletion
- context notes: data-retention-operator-owned

### ISO 27701 A.7.4.6: A.7.4.6 Temporary files

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Organization shall ensure that temporary files created as a
result of processing of PII are disposed of (e.g., erased,
destroyed) following documented procedures within a specified,
documented period.

**What Pryv does for you**

Temporary-file handling is an operating-system / runtime concern.
Pryv-the-software doesn't write PII to ad-hoc temp files; the
operator's host hygiene (tmpfs, /tmp cleanup, log rotation)
addresses any temp-file footprints the runtime produces.

### ISO 27701 A.7.4.9: A.7.4.9 Records of transfer of PII

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Organization shall record transfers of PII to or from third
parties and ensure cooperation with those parties to support
future requests related to obligations to PII principals.

**What Pryv does for you**

Cross-party PII transfers in Pryv go through accesses (typically
CMC capability accesses or shared accesses). Each access's
`clientData` records recipient + purpose + legal basis at grant
time; audit log captures each transfer event with timestamp.
Together they constitute the §164.528-style accounting record
for transfers specifically.

**Evidence**

- tests: AT01, AT51, AT61
- derives from: gdpr.Art.30, gdpr.Art.44, hipaa-privacy.164.528
- primitives: access, clientData, audit, CMC

### ISO 27701 A.7.5.1: A.7.5.1 Identify basis for PII transfer between jurisdictions

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: Organization shall identify and document the relevant basis for
transfers of PII between jurisdictions.

**What Pryv does for you**

Per GDPR Art. 44 /
Swiss nLPD Art. 34 mapping, the data-residency primitive
constrains where data lives; cross-jurisdictional transfers
record the legal basis on the transferring access's
`clientData.transfer_basis`. The jurisdiction-mapping
documentation (which jurisdictions appear in your deployment,
which transfer regime applies to each pair) is operator-side.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.44, gdpr.Art.46, gdpr.Art.49
- primitives: data-residency, access, clientData

### ISO 27701 A.7.5.2: A.7.5.2 Countries and international organizations to which PII can be transferred

Coverage: configurable · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Organization shall specify and document the countries and
international organizations to which PII can possibly be
transferred.

**What Pryv does for you**

`auth.hostings` declares the hostings (and thus countries /
jurisdictions) where subjects' data may live; for CMC
cross-platform sharing, the catalogue of trusted peer
deployments + their hostings is operator-managed. The
Statement-of-Applicability entry for A.7.5.2 cites the
`auth.hostings` config as the technical artefact.

**Evidence**

- tests: REGC, RC01, RC03
- config keys: auth.hostings
- primitives: data-residency, CMC

### ISO 27701 B.8.5.6: B.8.5.6, Disclosure of subcontractors used to process PII

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: awareness · draft

Requirement: Processor shall disclose to the customer in advance the use of
subcontractors before such subcontractors process PII; processor
shall publicly publish a list of subcontractors, or make it
available on request.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv-the-software has one
optional subprocessor surface, the observability provider (New
Relic adapter; default disabled). The operator's subcontractor
list typically includes: hosting provider, observability
provider when enabled, any backup-storage provider used by
`bin/backup.js` outputs. The operator publishes the list per
their B.8.5.6 commitment.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.28
- primitives: observability-provider

### ISO 27701 A.7.2.3: A.7.2.3 Determine when and how notice should be provided

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Organization shall determine when and how notice shall be
provided to PII principals concerning processing of their PII.

**What Pryv does for you**

Notice timing + form are
editorial. Pryv preserves whatever notice is shown (in
`access.clientData.privacy_notice` or dedicated
`consent/notice-*` event) so the same content is auditable per
principal per time.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27701.A.7.3.4, gdpr.Art.12, gdpr.Art.13
- primitives: access, clientData, app-web-auth3

### ISO 27701 A.7.2.4: A.7.2.4 Obtain and record consent

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Organization shall obtain and record consent from PII principals
according to the documented processes.

**What Pryv does for you**

Consent recording = `accesses.create` with permissions +
clientData carrying the consent text; cross-account consent =
`consent/request-cmc` events. The access keeps every previous
version; an event keeps its previous versions only with
`versioning.forceKeepHistory: true` (off by default), so the §7
demonstrability requirement is structural for the access and,
for the request event, holds as long as your app does not edit
it or history is on. Since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.38 the principal's
cross-account accept records the channels the relationship got
(`features`, resolved from the offer, which the accept may only
narrow) `[HA43]`, `[CD28]`, an account cannot record a consent to
its own offer (`cmc-self-accept-forbidden`) `[HA46]`, `[CN67]`,
and the server-written parts of the record survive a concurrent
client update `[ESR1]`. See `context/cmc-consent-primitives.md`.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA01, ACCP, HA43, CD28, HA46, CN67, ESR1
- derives from: gdpr.Art.7, iso-27701.A.7.3.4
- primitives: access, permissions, clientData, CMC, event
- context notes: cmc-consent-primitives

### ISO 27701 A.7.2.5: A.7.2.5 Privacy impact assessment

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: Organization shall assess the need for + implement a privacy
impact assessment whenever new processing of PII or changes to
existing processing are planned.

**What Pryv does for you**

PIA / DPIA is a written
assessment artefact. Pryv contributes the inputs (audit +
access primitives describe the processing flow; data-residency
primitive describes where data lives). Cross-link to gdpr.Art.35
+ swiss-nlpd.Art.22 for the regulator-specific DPIA mappings.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.35, swiss-nlpd.Art.22
- primitives: audit, data-residency, access

### ISO 27701 A.7.2.6: A.7.2.6 Contracts with PII processors

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Organization shall have a written contract with any PII processor
that it uses, requiring the processor to implement appropriate
controls.

**What Pryv does for you**

Contracts are out-of-scope; see GDPR Art. 28 + HIPAA-Security
§164.314(a)(1).

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.28

### ISO 27701 A.7.2.7: A.7.2.7 Joint PII controller

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Organization shall determine respective roles + responsibilities
where it acts jointly with one or more PII controllers.

**What Pryv does for you**

Joint-controller arrangements
(per GDPR Art. 26) get recorded on the relevant access's
`clientData.joint_controller_arrangement` with a pointer to the
written agreement. CMC's cross-platform access pattern is the
natural technical substrate for joint arrangements where each
controller runs their own Pryv deployment.

**Evidence**

- primitives: access, clientData, CMC

### ISO 27701 B.8.2.1: B.8.2.1, Customer agreement

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Customer agreement between processor and PII controller shall
address the processor's processing of PII consistent with
ISO/IEC 27018:2019 + applicable laws / regulations.

**What Pryv does for you**

Customer agreement = the DPA. Contractual, no software role.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.28

### ISO 27701 B.8.3.1: B.8.3.1, Obligations to PII principals

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Processor shall provide the customer (PII controller) with the
means to comply with its obligations to PII principals (right of
access, rectification, erasure, etc.).

**What Pryv does for you**

The standard Pryv API (events.get / events.update / streams.get
/ accesses.get / system.users.delete) gives the customer the
means to fulfill each principal-rights obligation directly.
The controller wraps these in their subject-portal; the
processor (Pryv operator) doesn't intermediate.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA01, EGSQ, UZEV, PTU1, USAD
- derives from: iso-27701.A.7.3.1, gdpr.Art.15, gdpr.Art.16, gdpr.Art.17, gdpr.Art.20
- primitives: access, event, stream, audit, data-types

### ISO 27701 B.8.4: B.8.4, Privacy by design and by default

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: high · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: Processor shall ensure privacy + data-protection design + default
principles are implemented in processing of PII.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv's architecture
leans privacy-by-design (per-user isolation, least-privilege
permissions, system-streams separation, audit by default). The
processor inheriting these defaults satisfies B.8.4
structurally. See gdpr.Art.25 for the cross-link to the
detailed primitive mapping.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.25, swiss-nlpd.Art.7
- primitives: access, permissions, stream, system-streams

### ISO 27701 B.8.5.2: B.8.5.2, Records of PII disclosures to third parties

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Processor shall record disclosures of PII to third parties,
including what PII has been disclosed, to whom, and at what time.

**What Pryv does for you**

When the processor (Pryv operator) executes a third-party
disclosure (e.g., a CMC cross-platform share, a shared access
to a counterparty), the audit log records the API call with
access reference; the access's `clientData.recipient` +
`clientData.purpose` capture the "to whom" + "for what" fields.
Together they constitute B.8.5.2-compliant records.

**Evidence**

- tests: AT01, AT51, AT61
- derives from: iso-27701.A.7.4.9, hipaa-privacy.164.528, gdpr.Art.30
- primitives: audit, access, clientData, CMC


## Medical Device Regulation (MDR)

- Scope id: `mdr` (regulation)
- Jurisdiction: EU + EEA
- Version: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (consolidated, incl. 2023 amendments to transition periods) (2017-04-05)
- Official text: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/745/oj
- Layered on: gdpr
- Requirements: 23 (11 facilitated, 12 out-of-scope)
- Browse: https://pryv.github.io/compliance-matrix/#/scope/mdr

### MDR Art.10: General obligations of manufacturers

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: Manufacturers shall ensure devices are designed and manufactured in
accordance with the requirements of the Regulation; shall establish,
document, implement, maintain, keep up-to-date and continually
improve a QMS that ensures compliance.

**What Pryv does for you**

MDR Art. 10 is the umbrella
obligation tying every other requirement to the manufacturer's
QMS. Pryv supplies the technical raw material that several QMS
sub-processes draw on (audit log for design controls +
post-market data; observability for system-status evidence;
backup-restore for data-integrity controls). The QMS itself is
the manufacturer's organizational artefact, see ISO 13485
scope for that side.

**Detail**

§10(1) compliance "with the requirements of this Regulation" is a
programme. §10(9) requires the QMS cover at minimum: strategy for
regulatory compliance, risk management, clinical evaluation, design
and manufacturing, post-market surveillance, communication,
vigilance reporting, management of CAPAs, monitoring + measurement
of output. Pryv contributes inputs to several of these, none can
be discharged by Pryv alone.

**Evidence**

- primitives: audit, observability-provider, backup-restore

### MDR Art.51: Classification of devices

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Devices shall be divided into classes I, IIa, IIb and III, taking
into account the intended purpose of the devices and their
inherent risks. Classification shall be carried out in accordance
with Annex VIII.

**What Pryv does for you**

Classification is a regulatory decision by the manufacturer (with
Notified Body involvement from class IIa upwards). Pryv is not a
medical device itself, when an implementer builds a device on
Pryv, the device's classification is determined by its own
intended purpose. Pryv has no contribution and no implementer
obligation arises from this Article alone.

### MDR Art.52: Conformity assessment procedures

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Manufacturers of devices, other than custom-made devices, shall
undertake an assessment of the conformity of those devices in
accordance with the applicable conformity assessment procedures
set out in Annexes IX-XI.

**What Pryv does for you**

Conformity assessment (technical documentation + clinical
evaluation + QMS audit by a Notified Body for class IIa+) is the
manufacturer's process. Pryv may appear in the technical
documentation as a sub-system supplier, but the conformity
decision is the manufacturer's. No software contribution from
Pryv at this layer.

### MDR Art.61: Clinical evaluation

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: Confirmation of compliance with relevant general safety + performance
requirements set out in Annex I shall be based on clinical data
providing sufficient clinical evidence.

**What Pryv does for you**

Clinical evaluation is the
manufacturer's regulatory artefact. Pryv's contribution is
operational: if your device collects clinical data during the
evaluation, Pryv stores it (events with stable class/format
from data-types) and audit-logs its processing, making the
clinical data set inspectable and reproducible.

**Detail**

The post-market clinical follow-up (PMCF) plan under Annex XIV B
drives ongoing data collection. Pryv as the data backend gives
you a single, audit-trailed substrate for both the pre-market
clinical evaluation file and the PMCF data feed.

**Evidence**

- primitives: audit, event, stream, data-types

### MDR Art.62: General requirements regarding clinical investigations

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: Clinical investigations on devices shall be designed and conducted
to ensure rights, safety, dignity and well-being of subjects;
data shall be reliable and robust.

**What Pryv does for you**

Subject protection in
clinical investigations rides on the same Pryv primitives that
carry GDPR Art. 32, per-subject storage isolation, access
control, audit, encryption at rest, restoration. "Reliable and
robust" data is the manufacturer's burden; audit-logged +
version-preserved Pryv events are the substrate.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.32
- primitives: access, audit, encryption-at-rest-secrets, backup-restore

### MDR Art.83: Post-market surveillance system of the manufacturer

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: Manufacturers shall plan, establish, document, implement, maintain
and update a post-market surveillance (PMS) system in a manner
proportionate to the risk class and appropriate for the type of
device.

**What Pryv does for you**

PMS data sources are
two-fold: (1) operational telemetry of the device + backend
(audit log + observability telemetry when enabled); (2) field
data from the device itself, captured as events. Pryv is the
substrate for both. The PMS plan itself, its trend analysis,
and the PSUR write-up under Art. 86 are manufacturer-side.

**Detail**

Pryv's audit log gives you the "what was processed, by whom,
when" timeline for the backend layer of the device. The
observability adapter (when enabled) gives system-availability
+ error-rate metrics, useful PMS indicators. For device-side
incident events (user-reported issues, on-device errors etc.),
the device pushes them as Pryv events on a dedicated stream.

**Evidence**

- primitives: audit, observability-provider, event

### MDR Art.85: Post-market surveillance report

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: Manufacturers of class I devices shall prepare a post-market
surveillance report summarising the results and conclusions of
the analyses of the post-market surveillance data.

**What Pryv does for you**

The PMS report itself is an
editorial artefact the manufacturer drafts. Pryv contributes
the data: audit log gives the backend activity summary; events
on the PMS streams give the field data summary. Composition of
the report is yours.

**Evidence**

- primitives: audit, event

### MDR Art.86: Periodic safety update report

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: Manufacturers of class IIa, IIb and III devices shall prepare a
periodic safety update report (PSUR) summarising the results +
conclusions of analyses of post-market surveillance data.

**What Pryv does for you**

Same Pryv contribution as
Art. 85, with cadence increased per device class (annually for
IIa+; available to competent authorities; for class III +
implantables, uploaded into Eudamed). The PSUR's analytical
content remains manufacturer-side.

**Evidence**

- primitives: audit, event, observability-provider

### MDR Art.87: Reporting of serious incidents and field safety corrective actions

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: Manufacturers shall report any serious incident involving devices
made available on the Union market, except expected side-effects
which are clearly documented in the product information.

**What Pryv does for you**

The reporting decision + the
report itself are manufacturer-side. Pryv's audit log +
observability data make root-cause analysis tractable when
investigating an incident, particularly when the incident's
chain of causation touches the backend (e.g., a latency spike
correlated to a clinical decision). The 15-day / 10-day / 2-day
reporting timelines are operational.

**Evidence**

- primitives: audit, event, observability-provider

### MDR A1.17: Annex I §17 Electronic programmable systems / software

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: Devices that incorporate electronic programmable systems, including
software, or software that are devices in themselves, shall be
designed to ensure repeatability, reliability and performance
according to their intended use.

**What Pryv does for you**

Annex I §17 is the General
Safety + Performance Requirement (GSPR) most directly relevant
to software medical devices. Pryv as the backend contributes to
several §17 sub-clauses: §17.2 (development and manufacture in
accordance with state-of-the-art principles), §17.4 (verification
and validation, audit log enables it), §17.5 (interaction with
mobile platforms, out of Pryv scope, app-side).

**Detail**

Per §17 sub-clause:
  - §17.1 Repeatability/reliability/performance, Pryv's audit log
    + reproducible-deployment posture (Docker image + multi-core
    HA) supports the manufacturer's V+V evidence.
  - §17.2 State-of-the-art SDLC, IEC 62304 alignment is
    manufacturer-side. Pryv's own release process (Dockerfile,
    test matrix, CHANGELOGs) feeds the manufacturer's supplier
    assessment.
  - §17.3 Risk management throughout the software lifecycle,
    ISO 14971-aligned; manufacturer-side. Pryv-side risk artefacts
    (e.g., this matrix + the QMS) inform supplier assessment.
  - §17.4 Verification and validation, audit log + the
    compliance-matrix test-citation chain are concrete evidence.

**Evidence**

- primitives: audit, backup-restore, multi-core-mTLS, letsEncrypt-integration, observability-provider

### MDR A1.18: Annex I §18 Active devices / connected devices

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Active devices and devices connected to them shall be designed in
such a way as to remove or reduce as far as possible the risks
relating to electrical, mechanical or thermal hazards.

**What Pryv does for you**

Annex I §18 covers physical electrical/mechanical/thermal hazards,
outside Pryv's scope as a backend service. When the device
depends on Pryv for safe operation (e.g., a connected clinical
monitor), §18.4 + §18.7 (interoperability + connection-loss
safety) become operational concerns the manufacturer addresses
at the device + integration layer.

### MDR A1.23: Annex I §23 Information supplied with the device

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: The instructions for use and label of a device shall comply with
defined requirements (§23.1 labels, §23.2 IFU content, §23.3
e-labelling, §23.4 patient implant card content where applicable).

**What Pryv does for you**

Labelling + IFU content is the device manufacturer's editorial
artefact. Pryv has no role at the IFU-content layer. For
software medical devices that present the IFU in-app, the IFU
versioning + acknowledgement record can ride on Pryv events
with `clientData.ifu_version`, but the IFU content is
manufacturer-side.

### MDR Art.27: Unique Device Identification (UDI) system

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Manufacturers shall assign a UDI to their devices and place it on
the device label (or its packaging) before placing on the market;
record the UDI in their internal device-file system; submit it
to the UDI database (Eudamed UDI module).

**What Pryv does for you**

UDI assignment + Eudamed submission are manufacturer-side. Pryv
doesn't ship with a UDI (Pryv is not itself a medical device).
When a device built on Pryv has a UDI, the manufacturer's UDI
record may cite Pryv as a sub-system component but the UDI
management is theirs.

### MDR Art.93: Market surveillance activities (competent authorities)

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Competent authorities shall perform appropriate checks on the
conformity characteristics + performance of devices, including
review of documentation, physical / laboratory checks on
adequate samples, follow-up of received vigilance information.

**What Pryv does for you**

Market surveillance is competent-authority activity. Pryv has no
software role. If an authority requests information about the
Pryv-backed device, the manufacturer's evidence pack (drawing
on this matrix + the audit log) is the substrate of the
response.

### MDR Art.95: Measures required to deal with devices presenting an unacceptable risk to health

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: Competent authorities may require manufacturers to take all
appropriate corrective actions where a device presents an
unacceptable risk; including withdrawal, recall, restrictions
on availability.

**What Pryv does for you**

A recall / withdrawal
decision is manufacturer + authority side. Pryv contributes:
audit log + observability data scope the affected user / device
population (which subjects' devices were active when the risk
was identified); the access primitive gives the technical
mechanism to disable the device's backend connectivity if
remote disable is part of the corrective action; events on a
`recall/*` stream carry the recall communication record per
affected subject.

**Evidence**

- primitives: audit, access, event, observability-provider

### MDR Art.84: Post-market surveillance plan

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: The post-market surveillance plan referred to in Art. 83 shall be
part of the technical documentation specified in Annex II; details
in Annex III.

**What Pryv does for you**

The PMS plan document itself
is the manufacturer's artefact (it lives in the technical
documentation under Annex III). Pryv-side operational
contribution: when the plan calls for specific data collection
(e.g., field-event reporting cadence, telemetry thresholds),
the event-stream + audit substrate carries the data flow per
the plan. The plan's content (criteria, methods, cadence) is
manufacturer-side.

**Evidence**

- derives from: mdr.Art.83, iso-13485.4.2.5
- primitives: event, stream, audit, backup-restore

### MDR A2.5: Annex II §5 Information supplied by the manufacturer

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Technical documentation shall include a complete set of information
supplied with the device (labels, IFU, design history file
summary, post-market documentation references).

**What Pryv does for you**

The technical documentation
file (TDF) is the manufacturer's regulatory artefact. Pryv-side
support: events on a designated `tdf/<device-id>/*` stream with
attachments give a single, versioned, backed-up + audit-trailed
home for the file's contents. Cross-link to iso-13485.7.3.10
(design + development files) preserves the QMS standard's
parallel obligation.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-13485.7.3.10, mdr.A1.23
- primitives: event, stream, backup-restore

### MDR Art.5: Placing on the market and putting into service

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: A device may be placed on the market or put into service only if
it complies with this Regulation when duly supplied and properly
installed, maintained and used in accordance with its intended
purpose.

**What Pryv does for you**

Placing-on-market is the manufacturer's act and depends on the
device passing classification + conformity assessment. Pryv has
no role in the act itself.

### MDR Art.11: Authorised representative

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Where manufacturer is not established in a Member State, the
device may only be placed on the Union market if the manufacturer
designates an authorised representative.

**What Pryv does for you**

Authorised-representative designation is a contractual + Eudamed-
registration step for non-EU manufacturers. No software role.

### MDR Art.31: Registration of manufacturers, authorised representatives + importers

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Manufacturers, authorised representatives + importers shall
submit specified information to Eudamed.

**What Pryv does for you**

Eudamed registration is a regulatory submission. No software
role.

### MDR Art.55: Implant card and information to be supplied to the patient with an implanted device

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Manufacturer of an implantable device shall supply with the
device an implant card carrying device identification + patient-
specific safety information.

**What Pryv does for you**

Implant cards are physical artefacts (or digital equivalents
issued at implantation). If a digital implant-card record lives
in Pryv, the manufacturer puts it on a designated
`implant-card/*` stream, but the regulatory burden remains
manufacturer-side.

### MDR Art.14: General obligations of importers

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Importers shall verify that devices have been CE-marked + the
EU declaration of conformity drawn up, manufacturer + authorised
representative are identified, and importer's name + registered
trade name + address + place of business / single registered
office + UDI are indicated on device labelling or accompanying
documentation.

**What Pryv does for you**

Importer obligations are contractual + regulatory. No software
role.

### MDR Art.15: General obligations of distributors

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Distributors shall act with due care + verify CE marking,
EU declaration of conformity, language requirements, expiry
dates, etc. Shall cooperate with manufacturers and competent
authorities + maintain a register of complaints, non-conforming
devices, recalls + withdrawals.

**What Pryv does for you**

Distributor obligations are operational. No software role; if a
distributor uses Pryv to store its complaints + recall register,
see the iso-13485.4.2.5 control-of-records row.


## Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (Canada) (PIPEDA)

- Scope id: `pipeda` (regulation)
- Jurisdiction: Canada (federal, private sector)
- Version: S.C. 2000, c. 5 (consolidated, incl. Digital Privacy Act 2015 amendments) (2001-01-01)
- Official text: https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/p-8.6/
- Requirements: 13 (4 implemented, 1 configurable, 7 facilitated, 1 out-of-scope)
- Browse: https://pryv.github.io/compliance-matrix/#/scope/pipeda

### PIPEDA Principle.4.1: Schedule 1, Principle 1, Accountability

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: Organization is responsible for personal information under its
control and shall designate an individual or individuals who are
accountable for compliance with the following principles.

**What Pryv does for you**

Accountable-individual
designation is HR / organizational. Pryv contributes the
substrate the designated officer uses to demonstrate compliance:
audit log, observability, this matrix. Equips the role; doesn't
replace it.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.24, gdpr.Art.37, iso-27701.A.7.2.1
- primitives: audit, access, observability-provider

### PIPEDA Principle.4.2: Schedule 1, Principle 2, Identifying Purposes

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Purposes for which personal information is collected shall be
identified by the organization at or before the time the
information is collected.

**What Pryv does for you**

Per-access
`clientData.purpose` records the identified purpose at the moment
the access is minted (which is "at or before the time the
information is collected" for the access's scope). The purpose
vocabulary is editorial.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.5, iso-27701.A.7.2.1
- primitives: access, clientData

### PIPEDA Principle.4.3: Schedule 1, Principle 3, Consent

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Knowledge and consent of the individual are required for the
collection, use, or disclosure of personal information, except
where inappropriate.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv's access primitive IS the durable consent record,
versioned permissions + clientData (carrying the consent text +
knowledge-of-purpose disclosure) together prove what was
authorised. Withdrawal is `accesses.delete` or scope-down via
`accesses.update`; the version chain proves the timing. CMC
`consent/*` events handle cross-account flows.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA01, AA02, ACCP
- derives from: gdpr.Art.7, iso-27701.A.7.2.4, ccpa.1798.120
- primitives: access, permissions, clientData, CMC, event

### PIPEDA Principle.4.4: Schedule 1, Principle 4, Limiting Collection

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Collection of personal information shall be limited to that which
is necessary for the purposes identified by the organization.
Information shall be collected by fair and lawful means.

**What Pryv does for you**

Per-stream permissions limit what each access can write,
data outside an access's scope cannot reach Pryv via that access.
Stream-topology design (separating purposes onto distinct
subtrees) gives the granularity for "necessary for the
identified purposes". The fairness + lawfulness of the
collection method is editorial.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA01, ACCP
- derives from: gdpr.Art.5, iso-27701.A.7.4.1, ccpa.1798.140
- primitives: access, permissions, stream

### PIPEDA Principle.4.5: Schedule 1, Principle 5, Limiting Use, Disclosure, and Retention

Coverage: configurable · effort saved: medium · draft

Requirement: Personal information shall not be used or disclosed for purposes
other than those for which it was collected, except with the
consent of the individual or as required by law. Shall be
retained only as long as necessary for the fulfilment of those
purposes.

**What Pryv does for you**

Limit-use enforced by permissions; limit-disclosure enforced by
access scope to recipient. Retention has the same
configurable engine-dependent erasure mechanics noted under
GDPR Art. 17 + HIPAA-Security §164.310(d)(1): SQLite per-user
file deletion vs PG row deletion + backup rotation.
Automatic / scheduled retention enforcement is **operator-
owned** for events and streams (Pryv ships no TTL primitive
for records; whole accounts are covered by account
auto-deletion, see detail); the operator's external
retention job composes `events.get toTime=<cutoff>` +
`events.delete` + audit-log inactivity oracle,
`context/data-retention-operator-owned.md`).

**Detail**

Account auto-deletion, since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.66
(`8521c8d5`, see gdpr.Art.5 §1(e)). For the account level,
"retained only as long as necessary" is a setting: your
inactivity preset (`account.autoDeletion.inactivity.defaultDays`,
default none) deletes accounts unused for that many days, its
clock starting the day it first applies (`[ACXP2]`), after
reminder mails (`[ACXP3]`) and at least 7 days after the first
notice (`[ACXP8]`), and each individual may schedule their own
account's deletion. A preset covers only plain accounts with an
email address (`[ACST14]`, `[ADSW9]`); state it in your privacy
policy. Event-level retention stays your retention job.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA02, ACCP, USAD, ACXP2, ACXP3, ACXP8, ACST14, ADSW9
- docs: customer-resources/account-auto-deletion.md
- config keys: storages.userAccountStorage.engine, user-account.delete, account.autoDeletion.inactivity.defaultDays, account.autoDeletion.reminders.minNoticeDays
- derives from: gdpr.Art.5, gdpr.Art.17, ccpa.1798.105, iso-27701.A.7.4.5
- primitives: access, permissions, event, stream, backup-restore, account-auto-deletion
- context notes: data-retention-operator-owned

### PIPEDA Principle.4.6: Schedule 1, Principle 6, Accuracy

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Personal information shall be as accurate, complete, and
up-to-date as is necessary for the purposes for which it is
to be used.

**What Pryv does for you**

`events.update` rectifies events (matching GDPR Art. 16); the
prior value is kept only on a deployment with
`versioning.forceKeepHistory: true` (off by default), while the
audit log records who rectified which event and when either way.
The "necessary for the purposes" determination is editorial.

**Evidence**

- tests: PTU1
- specs: EVENT.BASE
- derives from: gdpr.Art.5, gdpr.Art.16, iso-27701.A.7.4.3
- primitives: event

### PIPEDA Principle.4.7: Schedule 1, Principle 7, Safeguards

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: high · mode: infrastructure · draft

Requirement: Personal information shall be protected by security safeguards
appropriate to the sensitivity of the information.

**What Pryv does for you**

Multi-aspect safeguards
inherited from the same primitive set as GDPR Art. 32 +
HIPAA-Security § 164.312 + ISO 27001 A.8. The "appropriate to
sensitivity" judgement (which subset to enable, how strictly to
scope) is the operator's.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.32, hipaa-security.164.312(a)(1), iso-27001.A.8.20
- primitives: permissions, system-streams, letsEncrypt-integration, multi-core-mTLS, encryption-at-rest-secrets, MFA, backup-restore, audit

**Planned changes**

- feature: End-to-end encryption reframes the safeguards posture for high-sensitivity health data

### PIPEDA Principle.4.8: Schedule 1, Principle 8, Openness

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Organization shall make readily available to individuals specific
information about its policies and practices relating to the
management of personal information.

**What Pryv does for you**

Policy + practice text lives
on `access.clientData.privacy_notice` or as `consent/notice`
events, durably + per-subject + per-time recoverable. The
`app-web-auth3` template is the customer-facing surface where
the policy typically appears. Drafting the text is editorial.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.12, gdpr.Art.13, ccpa.1798.130
- primitives: access, clientData, app-web-auth3, event

### PIPEDA Principle.4.9: Schedule 1, Principle 9, Individual Access

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Upon request, an individual shall be informed of the existence,
use, and disclosure of their personal information and shall be
given access to that information. An individual shall be able
to challenge the accuracy and completeness of the information
and have it amended as appropriate.

**What Pryv does for you**

Individual access is the same primitive surface as GDPR Art. 15 +
HIPAA-Privacy § 164.524 + CCPA § 1798.100: subject holding a
personal token reads events, streams, accesses (with history),
audit data via the standard Pryv API. Challenge-and-amend uses
`events.update` for amendments + the disagreement-statement-as-
event pattern for denied amendments.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA01, EGSQ, UZEV, PTU1
- specs: EVENT.BASE, STREAM.BASE
- derives from: gdpr.Art.15, gdpr.Art.16, hipaa-privacy.164.524, ccpa.1798.100
- primitives: access, stream, event, audit, data-types, account-backup-tool

### PIPEDA Principle.4.10: Schedule 1, Principle 10, Challenging Compliance

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: storage · draft

Requirement: Individual shall be able to address a challenge concerning
compliance with the above principles to the designated
individual or individuals accountable for the organization's
compliance.

**What Pryv does for you**

Complaint-intake workflow
stores each challenge as an event on a designated
`compliance/challenges/*` stream with disposition tracking. The
accountable-individual interaction + resolution workflow is
operator-side.

**Evidence**

- derives from: hipaa-privacy.164.530(d)
- primitives: event, stream, audit

### PIPEDA s.10.1: Division 1.1, Mandatory breach reporting (Digital Privacy Act 2015)

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: high · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: Organization shall report to the Privacy Commissioner any breach
of security safeguards involving personal information under its
control if it is reasonable in the circumstances to believe that
the breach creates a real risk of significant harm (RROSH).
Shall also notify affected individuals + maintain records of
every breach for at least 24 months.

**What Pryv does for you**

Same primitive set as the
parallel breach-notification regimes (GDPR Art. 33-34,
HIPAA-Breach §164.402-404, Swiss nLPD Art.24): the shipped
`bin/breach-scope.js` + audit log produce the RROSH-input
artefact (records affected, methods invoked, streams in scope)
in one command per compromised access; operator-side
at-rest encryption may bear on the RROSH determination
(HHS-equivalent safe-harbor reasoning, though RROSH is a
different test). The 24-month record-retention obligation rides
on Pryv events on a `compliance/breaches/*` stream.

**Detail**

RROSH factors include sensitivity of the PI involved + probability
that the PI has been / will be misused, both informed by
Pryv-side data (audit row method + access reference + clientData
categorization). The decision itself + reporting + notification
content + delivery are the operator's; record-keeping rides on
Pryv.

**Notification delivery** (s.10.1 "notify affected individuals"),
voluntarily missing + operator-owned at the platform layer.
Pryv ships the identification primitive (audit log + the
shipped `bin/breach-scope.js`); operator composes delivery
via their
existing CRM / mail / SMS pipeline. Per-recipient send-
receipts captured back as
`compliance/breach-notification/sent-cmc` events satisfy
the 24-month record-retention obligation on the same Pryv
event chain. Full pattern in
`context/breach-notification-delivery-operator-owned.md`.

**Evidence**

- derives from: gdpr.Art.33, gdpr.Art.34, hipaa-breach.164.402, hipaa-breach.164.404, swiss-nlpd.Art.24
- primitives: audit, encryption-at-rest-secrets, access, event
- context notes: breach-notification-delivery-operator-owned

**Planned changes**

- feature: Chained audit log improves RROSH evidence chain (scoping + non-repudiation)

### PIPEDA s.11: Right to file a complaint with the Privacy Commissioner

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Individual may file with the Commissioner a written complaint
against an organization for contravening a provision of Division
1 or for not following a recommendation set out in Schedule 1.

**What Pryv does for you**

Complaint-to-Commissioner is the individual's procedural right;
no software role on the Pryv side. The organization's response
file (the underlying evidence) draws on the audit log + this
matrix.

### PIPEDA framing: PIPEDA + provincial regimes, applicability

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: awareness · draft

Requirement: PIPEDA applies federally; provincial private-sector privacy acts
(BC PIPA, AB PIPA, Quebec Law 25) may apply in place of PIPEDA
to organizations operating substantially within those provinces.
Implementer determines which regime applies + may face multiple.

**What Pryv does for you**

Applicability is a legal
determination, not a software control. Pryv-side support: the
data-residency primitive lets you bind Canadian subjects' data
to a Canadian hosting (per-province granularity if multiple
Canadian hostings are configured), which simplifies the
substantially-within-province analysis. Tracking the chosen
regime per-deployment is operator-side.

**Evidence**

- primitives: data-residency


## SOC 2, AICPA Trust Services Criteria (Security, Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, Privacy) (SOC 2)

- Scope id: `soc2` (standard)
- Jurisdiction: United States (AICPA)
- Version: Trust Services Criteria (2017), with revised points of focus (2022) (2022-01-01)
- Official text: https://www.aicpa-cima.com/resources/landing/trust-services-criteria
- Requirements: 61 (8 implemented, 5 configurable, 38 facilitated, 10 out-of-scope)
- Browse: https://pryv.github.io/compliance-matrix/#/scope/soc2

### SOC 2 CC1.1: CC1.1 Commitment to integrity and ethical values

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: The entity demonstrates a commitment to integrity and ethical
values.

**What Pryv does for you**

Integrity + ethics are a management-and-culture matter. Pryv has
no software role at the values / code-of-conduct layer; your audit
log can later evidence whether workforce behaviour matched the
stated values, but the commitment itself is yours to make and
document.

### SOC 2 CC1.2: CC1.2 Board independence and oversight

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: The board of directors demonstrates independence from management
and exercises oversight of the development and performance of
internal control.

**What Pryv does for you**

Board governance is organizational. No software contribution; this
matrix + the audit log feed the oversight pack the board reviews,
but the oversight function is yours.

### SOC 2 CC1.3: CC1.3 Management structures, reporting lines, authorities

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: Management establishes, with board oversight, structures,
reporting lines, and appropriate authorities and responsibilities
in the pursuit of objectives.

**What Pryv does for you**

Org structure + authority assignment are management artefacts.
Pryv enforces the *technical* half of "appropriate authorities"
once you've decided them (see CC6.3 least-privilege), but the
reporting-line design itself is yours.

### SOC 2 CC1.4: CC1.4 Commitment to competence

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: The entity demonstrates a commitment to attract, develop, and
retain competent individuals in alignment with objectives.

**What Pryv does for you**

Hiring + training + retention is an HR programme. No software
role.

### SOC 2 CC1.5: CC1.5 Accountability for internal control responsibilities

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: The entity holds individuals accountable for their internal
control responsibilities in the pursuit of objectives.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv gives you the technical accountability substrate: every API
call is attributable to an access (accessId + accessSerial) in the
per-user audit log, so "who did what, when" is recoverable when
you need to hold an individual to account. Defining the
responsibilities and the consequence process is your management
activity; Pryv supplies the evidence trail.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27001.A.5.16
- primitives: audit, access

### SOC 2 CC2.1: CC2.1 Quality information to support internal control

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: The entity obtains or generates and uses relevant, quality
information to support the functioning of internal control.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv produces two streams of control-relevant information: the
per-user audit log (application-level activity, attributable to an
access) and observability metrics (operational + security KPIs via
the pluggable provider). What you monitor and how you act on it is
your programme; Pryv supplies the quality data.

**Evidence**

- primitives: audit, observability-provider

### SOC 2 CC2.2: CC2.2 Internal communication of objectives and responsibilities

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: The entity internally communicates information, including
objectives and responsibilities for internal control, necessary
to support the functioning of internal control.

**What Pryv does for you**

Internal communication of objectives is a management activity. No
software role at the communication-content layer.

### SOC 2 CC2.3: CC2.3 External communication on internal control matters

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: awareness · draft

Requirement: The entity communicates with external parties regarding matters
affecting the functioning of internal control.

**What Pryv does for you**

For the slice of external communication that concerns the Pryv
platform itself, open-pryv.io's public release process is the
channel: tagged releases, CHANGELOG-v2 + CHANGELOG-v2-back, and
(when shipped) the vulnerability-disclosure programme. You layer
your own customer / subprocessor / auditor communications on top.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27001.A.5.19
- primitives: audit

### SOC 2 CC3.1: CC3.1 Specifies objectives with sufficient clarity

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: The entity specifies objectives with sufficient clarity to enable
the identification and assessment of risks relating to objectives.

**What Pryv does for you**

Objective-setting is your management exercise. Pryv has no role in
authoring objectives; the matrix supports the downstream
risk-to-control mapping once your objectives exist.

### SOC 2 CC3.2: CC3.2 Identifies and analyzes risk

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: The entity identifies risks to the achievement of its objectives
across the entity and analyzes risks as a basis for determining
how the risks should be managed.

**What Pryv does for you**

Your risk-assessment methodology and the specific findings are
yours. Pryv contributes the inventory of technical controls (this
matrix, particularly the CC6 access + CC6.6/6.7 boundary +
cryptography rows), when you identify a confidentiality /
integrity / availability risk, the matrix surfaces which Pryv
primitive addresses it, so control applicability is mechanical
rather than judgemental.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27001.6.1.2
- primitives: access, permissions, audit, encryption-at-rest-secrets, multi-core-mTLS, backup-restore

### SOC 2 CC3.3: CC3.3 Considers the potential for fraud

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: The entity considers the potential for fraud in assessing risks
to the achievement of objectives.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv's audit log + observability metrics are the detection
substrate for insider-misuse and anomalous-access fraud scenarios
(every access is attributable; unusual read/write patterns
surface). The fraud-risk analysis itself, which scenarios matter,
what thresholds trigger review, is your assessment.

**Evidence**

- primitives: audit, observability-provider

### SOC 2 CC3.4: CC3.4 Identifies and assesses changes affecting internal control

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: The entity identifies and assesses changes that could
significantly impact the system of internal control.

**What Pryv does for you**

For changes to the Pryv platform, open-pryv.io's CHANGELOGs +
tagged releases announce what changed; the audit log shows when
config-driven behaviour changed observably in your deployment. The
change-impact assessment process is yours.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27001.A.8.32
- primitives: audit

### SOC 2 CC4.1: CC4.1 Performs ongoing and separate evaluations

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: The entity selects, develops, and performs ongoing and/or
separate evaluations to ascertain whether the components of
internal control are present and functioning.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv supplies the data an ongoing evaluation samples: the audit
log evidences control-effectiveness (e.g., that access scoping
actually blocks out-of-scope reads), observability evidences
operational health. You define the evaluation cadence and the
sampling method.

**Detail**

**A separate evaluation of the platform code.** The open-pryv.io
maintainers ran a code-level security review of the source in 2026
(2026-06 to 2026-10); its confirmed findings were fixed with
regression tests in open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.40 to 2.0.0-rc.51, each
described in the release notes. The public report,
`SECURITY-AUDIT.md`
(https://github.com/pryv/open-pryv.io/blob/master/SECURITY-AUDIT.md,
published 2026-10-14), lists each finding with its severity and fix
release and the known residual risks. Cite it as a supplier
evaluation of the software component; it does not evaluate your
deployment's controls, and it was not performed by an independent
party. See `context/code-security-review-2026.md`.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27001.A.8.16, iso-27001.9.1
- primitives: audit, observability-provider
- context notes: code-security-review-2026

### SOC 2 CC4.2: CC4.2 Evaluates and communicates deficiencies

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: low · mode: evidence · draft

Requirement: The entity evaluates and communicates internal control
deficiencies in a timely manner to those parties responsible for
taking corrective action.

**What Pryv does for you**

Pryv-side deficiency signals (audit anomalies, observability
alerts) feed your deficiency-tracking process. CAPA-style records
can themselves ride on Pryv events on a dedicated stream. The
evaluation + communication workflow is your procedure.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27001.10.2
- primitives: audit, observability-provider

### SOC 2 CC5.1: CC5.1 Selects and develops control activities

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: medium · mode: primitive · draft

Requirement: The entity selects and develops control activities that
contribute to the mitigation of risks to the achievement of
objectives to acceptable levels.

**What Pryv does for you**

Several of your control activities ARE Pryv primitives:
permission-scoped access tokens (purpose limitation), system
streams (privileged-data isolation), encryption of operator
secrets at rest. You select which to deploy against which risk;
Pryv provides the activities ready-made rather than as something
you build.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27001.A.8.27
- primitives: access, permissions, system-streams, encryption-at-rest-secrets

### SOC 2 CC5.2: CC5.2 General control activities over technology

Coverage: facilitated · effort saved: high · mode: primitive · draft

Requirement: The entity also selects and develops general control activities
over technology to support the achievement of objectives.

**What Pryv does for you**

The technology general controls SOC 2 examines, logical access,
authentication, encryption in transit + at rest for secrets,
audit logging, secure inter-core transport, are shipped Pryv
primitives, enforced at the API surface rather than left to your
configuration discipline. The CC6 + CC7 rows below detail each.
Your role is selecting and operating them.

**Evidence**

- derives from: iso-27001.A.8.3, iso-27001.A.8.24
- primitives: access, permissions, audit, letsEncrypt-integration, multi-core-mTLS, encryption-at-rest-secrets

### SOC 2 CC5.3: CC5.3 Deploys control activities through policies and procedures

Coverage: out-of-scope · draft

Requirement: The entity deploys control activities through policies that
establish what is expected and procedures that put policies into
action.

**What Pryv does for you**

Policy + procedure authoring is your editorial work. Pryv enforces
what the policies decide (access rules, encryption), but the
policy text and the operating procedures are yours.

### SOC 2 CC6.1: CC6.1 Logical access security over protected information assets

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: The entity implements logical access security software,
infrastructure, and architectures over protected information
assets to protect them from security events to meet the entity's
objectives.

**What Pryv does for you**

Logical access is enforced by Pryv at the API surface: every
read/write is checked against the access's per-stream + level
permissions, token-based authentication is the default, and MFA is
available via the mfa.* methods (on by default since open-pryv.io
2.0.0-rc.14 with authenticator-app TOTP; each account holder
enrols) `[MA15C]`, `[MA11A]`. System streams
isolate privileged data (credentials, MFA state). Transport
encryption is configured (in the core or at your proxy, see
CC6.7). You define who gets which access; Pryv enforces it.

**Detail**

**OAuth2 as a second logical-access path.** Alongside token +
MFA authentication, Pryv ships a standards-based OAuth2
authorization-code + PKCE authorization server
(`open-pryv.io/components/oauth2/`, open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.8):
discovery at `GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`,
`GET /oauth2/authorize`, and `POST /oauth2/token`. PKCE is
mandatory (S256 only); presented redirect URIs are validated by
exact string match with a single loopback-port carve-out
(RFC 8252 / 9700) and fragment-bearing redirect URIs are rejected
(`open-pryv.io/components/oauth2/src/clientRegistry.ts`). Client
registration is curated-only, the operator promotes an account
to an OAuth client via `bin/oauth-client.js`; open self-service
registration (`POST /oauth2/register`) is deliberately disabled.

**The OAuth2 surface since open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.64.** Added and
tested: token revocation (`POST /oauth2/revoke`, RFC 7009) and
introspection for clients registered `--can-introspect`
(`POST /oauth2/introspect`, RFC 7662), OpenID Connect discovery,
key set and id tokens when `oauth.signingKeys` lists a key (rc.69)
`[ORVK1]`, `[OXI01]`, `[OXD01]`; resource indicators (RFC 8707),
refused as `invalid_target` (rc.70) `[ORI03]`; token exchange for
resource servers registered `--can-exchange` (RFC 8693, rc.73)
`[OTX05]`; clients identified by a client metadata document URL
when `oauth.clientMetadataDocuments.mode` is not `off` (rc.74, see
CC6.2) `[OCMDE06]`. Since rc.74 the OAuth2 and discovery endpoints
answer CORS with their own policy (any origin, never credentials)
instead of the API's `[OACO1]`. Per-user addresses (rc.75) bind an
authorization to the account its address names `[OPUE2]`; with
`oauth.perUserIssuer` (rc.77, opt-in) each account host is its own
issuer `[OPIS4]`. The access-control effect of these is recorded on
CC6.3 and `hipaa-security.164.312(a)(1)`.

**Federated sign-in (SSO).** An account holder may also authenticate
through an external OpenID Connect provider (`sso.*`, beta, off by
default). It mints a normal Pryv session but is gated so an external
identity cannot claim an account whose email was never inbox-proved,
MFA (when active) is still enforced, and the session token reaches
the auth app via a one-time shared secret, never a URL. Sign-ins and
refusals are recorded in the audit trail (`sso.login`, `sso.refused`).

**Credential transmission to third parties.** When a credential
must be handed to a counterparty, the shared-secrets endpoints
(`open-pryv.io/components/shared-secrets/`) replace URL-embedded
tokens with a one-time random key: redeemable exactly once (with
atomic single-winner semantics under concurrent redemption),
mandatory TTL, only the SHA-256 of the key's random half stored
server-side, payload scrubbed when the item leaves the pending
state (on redemption, on a signature mismatch, and on the first
retrieval attempt after the TTL; expiry is enforced on access,
not by a background sweeper, so an untouched expired secret keeps
its payload until something reaches it or you delete it),
optional passphrase / HMAC signature on redemption. Browser history, referrer headers, and access logs
therefore stop carrying live credentials. A
`secretSharing: forbidden` feature permission, inherited by
child accesses and not strippable via `accesses.update`, lets
you exclude designated access classes from minting shared
secrets at all.

**Delegate-account access path.** Account delegation
(`open-pryv.io/components/delegation/`) lets one account hold an
owner-equivalent delegate token over another. It rides the same
per-stream permission enforcement as any token, and its logical-
access guarantee is the non-forgeable teardown: a delegate can
never remove a delegation, and dissolving one requires a genuine
login on the controlled account (a personal token with no
forge-protected delegation marker). The `:_delegation:*`
namespace is plugin-owned and guarded (no user create/write/
delete; internal subtree read-guarded and excluded from wildcard
reads); each delegate's actions are audited on the controlled
account. See `context/delegation-model.md`.

**Privileged streams, by every spelling of an id** (open-pryv.io
2.0.0-rc.56). The guards that isolate the account fields (the
primary email, written only through `account.update`; the
non-editable and hidden fields; the level caps on account-stream
permissions), the delegation namespace and the plugin-managed
regions of the cross-account (CMC) namespace judge the stream an
id resolves to, whatever store-prefixed spelling a request uses,
for every token `[ASA1]`, `[ASA2]`, `[ASA6]`, `[CNRP6]`,
`[CNRP7]`. Before this release a store-prefixed spelling was not
recognised by these guards, so the isolation held only for
requests using the canonical ids; in particular an access holding
`contribute` on the email field could change the primary email
through the events API.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA01, AA02, ACCP, MA15C, MA11A, SHS02, SHS09, SHS13, ASA1, ASA2, ASA6, CNRP6, CNRP7, ORVK1, OXI01, OXD01, ORI03, OTX05, OCMDE06, OACO1, OPUE2, OPIS4
- docs: customer-resources/auth-oauth2.md
- config keys: oauth.signingKeys, oauth.clientMetadataDocuments.mode, oauth.perUserIssuer
- derives from: iso-27001.A.5.15, iso-27001.A.8.5, hipaa-security.164.312(a)(1)
- primitives: access, permissions, system-streams, MFA, encryption-at-rest-secrets, letsEncrypt-integration, shared-secrets, delegation
- context notes: delegation-model

**Planned changes**

- enhancement: Reference TOTP / WebAuthn MFA plugins + AAL-tier mapping strengthen the CC6.1 authentication-strength evidence

### SOC 2 CC6.2: CC6.2 User registration, credential issuance, and de-provisioning

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: Prior to issuing system credentials and granting system access,
the entity registers and authorizes new internal and external
users whose access is administered by the entity. For those users
whose access is administered by the entity, user system
credentials are removed when user access is no longer authorized.

**What Pryv does for you**

The full credential lifecycle is Pryv primitives: registration
mints an account; accesses.create issues a scoped credential;
accesses.update modifies scope (writing the prior version to
history); accesses.delete revokes; system.users.delete removes the
account entirely. Each stage lands in the audit log. The
authorization decision (who may register, what scope is
appropriate) is your policy; the mechanism is shipped.

**Detail**

**OAuth2 client credential issuance is curated.** For
delegated-app credentials, Pryv issues OAuth2 client identities
only through the operator CLI (`bin/oauth-client.js`, register /
rotate-secret / list), not through open dynamic registration: the
discovery document advertises no registration endpoint and
`POST /oauth2/register` (RFC 7591 open mode) is intentionally
deferred, `oauth.clientRegistration.mode: curated` is the only
supported value and `open` is rejected. Each client carries an
exact-match set of registered redirect URIs and, for confidential
clients, a rotatable `client_secret`. The authorization decision
(who becomes a client, which redirect URIs + scopes are
appropriate) stays your policy; the issuance + rotation mechanism
is shipped (`open-pryv.io/components/oauth2/`, open-pryv.io
2.0.0-rc.8).

**Operator-registered clients and their vetting (open-pryv.io
2.0.0-rc.68 and 2.0.0-rc.71).** `bin/oauth-client.js
create-registry` registers a client for an installed OAuth
extension, with a mandatory subject type (`public` or `pairwise`,
no default), audiences, lifetimes, an optional region and a
secret, `private_key_jwt` keys or none (public, PKCE). Since rc.71
a change to what an active client may do (redirect URIs, scope,
keys, auth method, audiences, allowed features, lifetimes) moves
it to `review` until the operator approves it, and a client under
review or suspended is refused everywhere, the data API included
`[OCLI19]`, `[ORF1]`. A rotated secret can keep the previous one
valid for at most 30 days `[OCAK14]`; logos are shown only from
hosts listed in `oauth.logoHosts` `[ORF4]`.

**Correction and opt-in: client metadata documents (open-pryv.io
2.0.0-rc.74).** "Curated only" holds while
`oauth.clientMetadataDocuments.mode` is `off`, the default. With
`allowList` (hosts you list) or `any`, a client may identify itself
by an https URL whose JSON document Pryv fetches: identity and
display come from the document, reach comes only from your
`client` template (scope, audiences, subject type, lifetimes),
never from the document. Such a client can never hold a secret,
introspection, token exchange, allowed features or "any audience",
and authenticates with `none` or `private_key_jwt` only
`[OCMD01]`, `[OCMD05]`, `[OCMDE03]`, `[OCMDE06]`. The fetch is a
guarded outbound call (see `CC6.6`), every fetch and refusal is in
the audit trail without the document body (`oauth.client.
metadata_fetched` / `metadata_refused`) `[OCMDE13]`, and the
consent screen must show the client's host next to its name.
`mode: any` lets any party present a client to your users' consent
screen: prefer `allowList`, keep `deniedHosts` current. Open
registration (`POST /oauth2/register`) stays disabled in every
mode.

**Delegate-credential issuance + de-provisioning.** Account
delegation (`open-pryv.io/components/delegation/`) issues a
delegate an owner-equivalent personal token over another account
through a controlled-account-initiated invite / accept handshake
(the only no-credential step is the operator-admin-key-gated
invite); create-from-delegate can provision a fresh controlled
account at the same time. De-provisioning is authoritative and
reserved to the controlled account: a delegate can never remove a
delegation, and detach is gated on a genuine login of the
controlled account. Issuance and teardown are audited per
delegate on the controlled account (same-core + cross-core). See
`context/delegation-model.md`.

Credentials a delegate issues to apps for the controlled account
follow the same lifecycle: each is an ordinary app access on the
controlled account, marked by the server as granted through the
delegation `[DCH01]`, and they are removed together with the
delegation: detach deletes every access granted through it, and
nothing the account holder granted `[DCH12]`. So credentials
issued under a delegate's authority do not survive the end of
that authority. In open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.23.

**Group accounts over CMC** (open-pryv.io 2.0.0-rc.53, release
commit `61fb28dd`, https://github.com/pryv/open-pryv.io/issues/158).
For a team sharing one account, a member is registered and
authorized before any credential reaches them: the member's
membership request is accepted by an administrator of the group
`[GA01]`, and only then can the member obtain, per patient, a
short-lived credential minted by the group's core and returned
once in the answer to the member's request, never stored, logged
or retried `[GA10]`, `[MA50]`; asking again with the same
permissions while it has more than five minutes left returns the
same access `[GA11]`, and any
other caller is refused (`cmc-member-access-not-member`)
`[GA12]`. When the membership ends, including when the delegate
who approved it is detached, the group's core deletes those
credentials on every patient account and records the outcome
`[GA20]`, `[GA22]`, `[GA23]`. See
`context/workforce-access-patterns.md`, Pattern 3.

**Evidence**

- tests: AA01, AA02, ACCP, UZEV, DCH01, DCH12, CMCGA, GA01, GA10, GA11, GA12, GA20, GA22, GA23, MA50, OCLI19, ORF1, OCAK14, ORF4, OCMD01, OCMD05, OCMDE03, OCMDE06, OCMDE13
- docs: customer-resources/auth-oauth2.md
- config keys: oauth.logoHosts, oauth.clientMetadataDocuments.mode, oauth.clientMetadataDocuments.allowedHosts, oauth.clientMetadataDocuments.deniedHosts, oauth.clientMetadataDocuments.client
- derives from: iso-27001.A.5.16, iso-27001.A.5.18, hipaa-security.164.308(a)(3)(ii)(C)
- primitives: access, system-streams, audit, delegation, CMC
- context notes: delegation-model, workforce-access-patterns

### SOC 2 CC6.3: CC6.3 Role-based access, least privilege, segregation of duties

Coverage: implemented · effort saved: high · draft

Requirement: The entity authorizes, modifies, or removes access to data,
software, functions, and other protected information assets based
on roles, responsibilities, or the system design and changes,
giving consideration to the concepts of least privilege and
segregation of duties, to meet the entity's objectives.

**What Pryv does for you**

Least privilege is native: an access carries only the
stream+level tuples it needs (none / create-only / read /
contribute / manage), so a credential cannot touch out-of-scope
data. Segregation of duties is expressed by issuing distinct
narrow accesses per role, with system streams isolating privileged
functions. accesses.update / .delete cover modify + remove; access
